articles.title: IIHF confirms cyberattack after website goes offline
articles.summary: The International Ice Hockey Federation has confirmed it has been targeted by a cyberattack, with the organization's website offline since Tuesday morning.

image.caption: A screengrab of the image that has appeared when loading the International Ice Hockey Federation website since early Tuesday. (IIHF.com)

blocks.text: World·New
The International Ice Hockey Federation has confirmed it has been targeted by a cyberattack, with the organization's website offline since Tuesday morning.
Attack comes days after federation confirmed Russia won't compete at next month's world juniors in Alberta

"We strongly condemn these actions and are taking all necessary steps to investigate the source of the attack and restore our systems," the IIHF said in a statement posted to social media Tuesday afternoon.
"Our platforms will be back online as soon as we are confident they are secure."
The cyberattack comes just days after the federation confirmed Russia would not compete at next month's world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

Multiple media reported that, early Tuesday morning, a pro-Russia image and caption appeared on the IIHF website. CBC News has not been able to confirm whether an image or message linked to Russia was posted.
The site has been offline since, displaying a notice saying it was "temporarily unavailable."
CBC News has contacted the IIHF for comment but has yet to hear back.

items: IIHF confirms Russia not competing at world juniors next month in Alberta
Canadian government says Russian players with visas will still be barred from WJC

blocks.text: Russia and Belarus have been banned from competing in international hockey tournaments since 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine that year. But last month, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled Russia must be allowed back into the ice hockey world championships.
Despite this, Canada announced it was barring Russian players from competing in the world juniors.

"Canada’s position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual. Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine," Secretary of Sport Adam van Koeverden said in a statement provided to CBC News.
Team Russia won't compete at World Juniors in Alberta
On Sunday, the IIHF confirmed Russia will not have a team at the championship, citing Canada's restrictions. They added that Canada will remain as host despite going against CAS's ruling.

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable" and "unlawful," and demanded the tournament be removed from Canada. Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev called for "consequences" that would affect Canada hosting future sports events.
CBC News has contacted Hockey Canada but has yet to hear back.
This year's world junior championship in Edmonton and Red Deer begins Dec. 26. Sweden claimed the gold medal at last year's tournament in Minnesota, while Canada took home bronze.

Canada's Connor Bedard scores on Russia goalie Yegor Guskov during an IIHF World Junior Hockey Championship exhibition game in Edmonton in December 2021. The federation recently confirmed Russia will not have a team at the world junior hockey championship next month in Alberta. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

articles.title: St Kitts and Nevis fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship-by-investment program
articles.summary:
Prime minister of twin-island Caribbean nation announces program wind-down after EU threatens to end visa-free access

The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering…

blocks.text: The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.

On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.

Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.

The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.

In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.

In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.

He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.

“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.

The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy is “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.

“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.

Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

image.caption: Rockstar's upcoming release, Grand Theft Auto VI — pictured here — received eight nominations for the Game Awards. (Rockstar Games)

blocks.text: Grand Theft Auto VI has yet to be released to the general public, but already it's being touted as the potential game of the year.
The Game Awards released its nomination list for 2026 on Tuesday, with Grand Theft Auto VI receiving eight — the most nominations for a single game with eight — including Game of the Year.
The game, which releases Nov. 19, slipped under the wire, as games needed to be available by Nov. 20 to be considered.
Nintendo received the most nominations for a single publisher, with 12, for games including The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and Pokémon Pokopia.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' or 'Lying King'? Aiden Pleterski says he was neither at alleged kidnappers' trial
articles.summary: Aiden Pleterski denied ever calling himself the "Crypto King" — or paying for a Forbes sponsored article that did — under cross-examination at the trial for his alleged kidnappers in Toronto on…

image.caption: Under cross-examination Tuesday, Aiden Pleterski said he'd never promoted himself as the 'Crypto King.' (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

Aiden Pleterski denied ever calling himself the "Crypto King" — or paying for a Forbes sponsored article that did — under cross-examination at the trial for his alleged kidnappers in Toronto on Tuesday.
Defence lawyer suggests Pleterski can't be trusted in cross-examination
"You weren't the Crypto King, you were the Lying King, you were taking other people's money and spending it on yourself," said defence lawyer Hussein Aly in Ontario Superior Court.
"I don't think I'm a king at all, and I disagree with that," replied Pleterski. He repeated in court that he'd never called himself the Crypto King even once.

Pleterski was convicted of fraud last month in connection with more than $30 million he took from investors to trade on their behalf, but he has yet to be sentenced. The 27-year-old told the court Tuesday he disagreed with that decision.

Akil Heywood, Alfredo Paladino and Rakeem Henry are all charged with kidnapping and extorting Pleterski over the course of three days in early December 2022. Pleterski testified to being beaten and tortured by his alleged kidnappers in various locations across southern Ontario as they questioned him about where his money was.

Alfredo Paladino, Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry (from left to right) are accused of kidnapping and extorting the self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski in December 2022. (Evan Mitsui/CBC, atlanticmastoronto/Instagram, Evan Mitsui/CBC)

The Crown alleges Heywood was one of Pleterski's investors who lost a significant amount of money and was the "driving force" behind the plan to kidnap him, while Paladino and Henry were allegedly involved in carrying it out.
Paladino and Henry are also charged with firearms offences, the aggravated assault of Pleterski, assaulting him with a weapon, and assault causing bodily harm over that same period.
All three men have pleaded not guilty.

items: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies about escape attempt during alleged kidnapping
'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies he was beaten, tortured during alleged kidnapping
Crypto King's alleged kidnappers’ trial hears call Aiden Pleterski made to landlord asking for $3M

blocks.text: Aly, who is representing Heywood, began his cross-examination of Pleterski Tuesday morning.

Before the court broke for lunch Tuesday, he'd called Pleterski the "Lying King" multiple times and ran the court through several examples of Pleterski's alleged lies from his fraudulent investment scheme and his bankruptcy proceedings.
Those included a screenshot of a $311 million fund Pleterski provided to investors, which Pleterski admitted never existed.

Defence lawyer Hussein Aly entered this screenshot as an exhibit at the trial for three men accused of kidnapping Aiden Pleterski. Pleterski admitted the $311 million never existed. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)
"You're nothing but a liar, a cheat and a thief," said Aly to Pleterski in court. "Your religion is money. The only thing that matters to you in the world is money."
Pleterski denied both assertions.
Heywood's role in bankruptcy

The Crown entered copies of wire transfers and bank drafts as exhibits Tuesday morning showing that Heywood transferred Pleterski $300,000 in November 2021. And later, Pleterski's company transferred Heywood funds twice for a total of $250,000.
Aly also questioned Pleterski on how he ended up bankrupt in 2022.
"Your whole Ponzi scheme fell apart because someone went to the courts," he said to Pleterski.
Pleterski disagreed with calling it a Ponzi scheme, but said the "first two individuals who sued me were Sacha Singh and I believe Akil Heywood as well."
Aly said his client used lawful means to address his missing funds by taking Pleterski to court.
"You didn't go into bankruptcy, they forced you into bankruptcy," said Aly.
Again, Pleterski disagreed.
"You were mad at Akil Heywood, because of Heywood, no more private jets," said Aly.
Aiden Pleterski posted this photo of himself on a private jet to his own Instagram account. (aiden.ptrs/Instagram)

Earlier in his cross-examination Aly walked the jury through summaries of Pleterski's financial records which were used as evidence in his fraud trial and others from his bankruptcy. Those records showed he took in about $40 million dollars and spent over $13.5 million on lifestyle expenses, including on private jets and luxury cars.
Texts night of alleged kidnapping

Aly also entered a text message exchange between Pleterski's phone and Heywood's as an exhibit, which was time stamped 11:50 p.m. on Dec. 5, 2022. Based on the Crown's evidence at trial so far, and Pleterski's prior testimony, he said he was already kidnapped by that time that day.
This is a transcript of the text exchange:
Aiden Pleterski's phone: I have your money
Aiden Pleterski's phone: Don't worry ;)"
Aiden Pleterski's phone: Haha
Akil Heywood: I want it now
Aiden Pleterski's phone: Sorry for ripping u off for 7 mill
Aiden Pleterski's phone: But it's tough being a big bitch
Akil Heywood: Yup I agree

Pleterski testified he didn't send those text messages and said they would have been sent by "Slime" during the kidnapping. "Slime" was the lead kidnapper, according to the Crown, but he is not part of this trial.
Aly is expected to continue his cross-examination Tuesday afternoon.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: ‘Heads should roll’: owner of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in skip bin demands probe
articles.summary:
Stuart Ramsey says it is a ‘bloody disgrace’ the gelding was left in the skip bin while awaiting burial

So You Are’s owner-breeder has demanded a full investigation after the Melbourne Cup…

blocks.text: So You Are’s owner-breeder has demanded a full investigation after the Melbourne Cup runner’s body was found in a skip at a Sydney tip, insisting “heads have got to roll”.
Stuart Ramsey says it is a “bloody disgrace” the gelding was left in the skip bin while awaiting burial at Sydney’s Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre.
The grisly sight was uncovered by a Sydney man, with online footage outraging industry participants and anti-horse racing activists alike.
Bjorn Baker’s promising stayer took ill at a spelling farm after finishing eighth in Australia’s most famous race on 3 November.

He was rushed to the REC Equine Specialists veterinary clinic at Horsley Park in Sydney’s west after showing signs of colic on Monday morning. Surgery could not save the horse and he was euthanised under anaesthesia.
Racing NSW said its ongoing investigations found So You Are was being held temporarily awaiting burial when the footage was recorded.

While REC has apologised, Ramsey, a renowned breeder at boutique Hunter Valley farm Turangga Stud, wants answers and accountability over the disposal of the five-year-old, who earned A$1.4m from eight career wins.
“There should be a full investigation. Heads have got to roll – simple as that,” Ramsey said.
“He was more than just a racehorse. He brought our family together, and to think of the stress the family are under now because of this – it’s a bloody disgrace.
“We took 30-odd people down to Melbourne for the race. So You Are brought us all together, as only a horse can do. It’s very sad that it’s happened.”

REC’s managing partner, Jonathan Lumsden, said the centre had spoken with So You Are’s owners and trainers to apologise. He said the veterinary practice did not carry out the burial, but took “full responsibility” for choosing the service provider and arrangements.
“He should have been promptly and respectfully buried,” Lumsden said in a statement.
Ramsey, who said he had not been contacted by REC, said he is not satisfied with their explanation.
“So they should take responsibility. It wasn’t the contractor’s fault; it was their fault. They were in charge of the horse,” he said.
“They didn’t even give us the option of burying him up at Turangga ... they should all be out – gone. I don’t mean everyone, but the bosses and the people who’ve made the decisions.”
Ramsey declared racehorses are among the best looked-after animals in the world and spoke of his affinity for So You Are. “He meant so much to us,” he said.
The treatment of So You Are’s remains has sparked strong criticism from animal welfare groups.
“There is always the option to bury the horse or have the horse cremated,” Elio Celotto, the campaign director for the Coalition for the Protection of Racehorses, said.
“However, it is more expedient to dump the horse at a local tip. This is business as usual for an industry where profit is always more important than sentiment.”
Georgie Purcell, a Victorian Animal Justice Party MP, said the tragic case should force the industry to confront serious questions about duty of care.
“The racing industry breeds these horses and profits from them but fails the most basic obligation to treat them with dignity after death,” she said.
Racing NSW said “appropriate action” would be taken if any wrongdoing was discovered in its ongoing investigation .
“Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process,” it said.
“That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner.”
Baker said he was also left deeply distressed by the handling of the much-loved horse’s remains, adding they deserved to be treated with dignity and respect.
Cleanaway were contacted for comment.

articles.title: An SNL sketch about caregiving has gone viral. B.C. caregivers explain why
articles.summary: What started as a joke on a late-night sketch comedy show quickly blew up online in the hours following its airing. It’s garnered more than 11.9 million views on Instagram alone, and shared hundreds…

image.caption: Women are still the default caregivers in many family situations, experts say, which is why the SNL sketch has resonated with people around the world. (Photographee.eu/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

What started as a joke on a late-night sketch comedy show quickly blew up online in the hours following its airing. It’s garnered more than 11.9 million views on Instagram alone, and shared hundreds of thousands of times.
Sister sketch has been seen and shared millions of times since it aired Nov. 14

Comedian John Mulaney stands in the middle of a generic home, his hand on the shoulder of Saturday Night Live cast member Tommy Brennan, who plays his father. Brennan's character can't remember if he took his pills.

"My dad means the world to me, so when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible," Mulaney begins. "I didn't want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aid could cost thousands a week. I didn't know where to turn.
"That's when I heard about Sister," says Mulaney, who describes the service as "a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister."
He goes on to say sisters often take on free, somewhat assumed labour to care for aging parents.
"And I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do," he adds.

The sketch quickly blew up online in the hours after it aired on Nov. 14. It’s garnered more than 12 million views on Instagram alone as of Tuesday afternoon, and shared hundreds of thousands of times.

Barbara MacLean, executive director of Family Caregivers of B.C., says the sketch certainly made the rounds in her office, and while the sketch is funny, there's a deeper message that isn't really funny at all.
Why SNL’s viral 'Sister' sketch hits a nerve with female caregivers in B.C.
It illustrates the ways some family members, often women, are the default caregivers for aging parents, she said.

"You see yourself in that sketch, you laugh, but then you say, 'Wow, this is me,'" MacLean said. "I think there's an awful lot of feeling that's attached to that because it speaks to so many aspects of the caregiving role."
Women carry mental load: MacLean

Carol Dowe, who founded a support group for caregivers on Vancouver Island, said the sketch likely resonated so broadly because baby boomers — of which there are about nine million in Canada, according to the 2021 census — are entering the age where they need care, and their kids are feeling the pressure. Especially women, she added.
"Women tend to be the ones that people turn to in the family," Dowe said.
More and more men are taking on caregiving roles, MacLean said. Statistics Canada data from 2024 suggests nearly half of caregivers are, in fact, men.

items: Changes to Canada's caregiver benefit 'an excellent step,' but more needed: advocates
Caregivers in region with Canada's oldest demographic call for more respite, seniors care

blocks.text: However, MacLean said women still carry most of the mental or emotional load of caring for others — not just aging family members. Things like planning ahead, knowing what's in the fridge, keeping track of medical appointments, work commitments, kids' activities — it all piles up, she said.
"Organizing the lives of everybody, the social conveners, the connectors. I think it's natural, you know, caregiving," MacLean said. "It's silent and it's invisible."

She said that while progress has been made, society has a ways to go in terms of equity for women. One way to make a change is to start conversations among family early, so that there's no surprise when mom or dad, or an aunt or uncle, does need assistance, MacLean said.
"That's where we'd love to see society go, and it's going there."
Dowe said caregivers, whether they're men or women, need a break, and she urges families to consider sharing the load.

"They're taking care of their loved one 24/7," Dowe said. "I mean it's everything from weight transfer, going to the bathroom, getting out of bed. And when you're constantly doing this 24 hours around the clock as a caregiver without a break, I mean it takes its toll. And we get edgy as caregivers. We can get angry."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Courtney Dickson is a journalist with CBC News based in Vancouver, covering stories throughout B.C. She has previously worked for CBC in Kamloops and Toronto. She has won Radio Television Digital News Association awards locally and nationally, and in 2022, won a Webster Award.

articles.title: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody
articles.summary:
Child reunited with family after he was detained by immigration agents in San Diego and transferred to Texas

An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by…

blocks.text: An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.

Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.

The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.

The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.

“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.

Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

US homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended his…

blocks.text: US homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended his decision to fly in a private government to a college football game on Saturday as Americans weathered widespread flight delays and cancellations, saying: “We still got to live our life.”

Mullin, a former US senator from Oklahoma, traveled on a government aircraft on Saturday to watch a football game between Louisiana State University and the University of Texas, the New York Post reported on Tuesday. The trip to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, came about a day after a four-hour ground stop that led to thousands of flights being delayed or cancelled – and an estimated 1.5 million people were stranded.
Evidently, botched maintenance work upgrading telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optic cables in at least one remote location prompted the FAA to implement the ground stop.

Mullin is required to travel on a government aircraft with secure communication systems and pay back the government for personal travel. Still, the homeland security secretary defended his decision to travel for pleasure while many other Americans were stranded.
“We would have never went if the airlines – if the airways – weren’t completely open. [And] they’d been completely open for 21 hours,” Mullin said on an interview on CNBC on Tuesday.
“I would have never taken airspace if the airspace wasn’t open and we still got to live our life at the same time.
“We still have family, friends, and we also have work we do every day.”

Mullin spent part of the game in the box of Ben Bordelon, CEO of Bollinger Shipping, a company that has Department of Homeland Security contracts, the Post reported. Mullin said on CNBC he did not know Bordelon.

He defended his travel as Republicans have sought to cast shift blame away from Donald Trump’s administration for the nationwide ground stop to Congress and the Joe Biden White House prior to Trump’s second presidency.
Democrats have said that characterization is “absurd”, noting that both the Biden administration and Congress have allocated tens of billions of dollars for air traffic control improvements.

articles.title: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers
articles.summary: Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the…

image.caption: Hashim Thaci (pictured here in court in 2023) stepped down as president of Kosovo nearly six years ago to defend himself against war crimes charges Image: Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP

blocks.text: A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.
Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.
Swift response from government

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.
Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

blocks.caption: The conviction in September of Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders was greeted with shock, disappointment and anger in KosovoImage: Ermal Meta/Matrix Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.
The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."
What is the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.
The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.
For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.
Government set up working group

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

blocks.caption: Speaking of Thaci's September conviction of war crimes in September, Prime Minister Albin Kurti has said that the government of Kosovo 'is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers' Image: Liam McBurney/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."
Parliament considers amending law
In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

blocks.caption: Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute stresses that there is a fundamental difference between criticism of courts based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courtsImage: Bekim Shehu/DW

blocks.text: "Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.
'Room for criticism of both sides'

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

Canada's National Public Alerting System is running tests of its Alert Ready system Wednesday across all provinces and territories. Alert Ready delivers alerts about critical events such as tornadoes, flooding, fires and Amber alerts.
Alert Ready test will be broadcast on TV, radio and delivered to wireless devices
There's (probably) no need to take cover if your phone, radio or television blasts out the telltale sounds of an emergency alert Wednesday.

Canada's National Public Alerting System is running tests of its Alert Ready system across all provinces and territories. Alert Ready delivers alerts about critical events such as tornadoes, flooding, fires and Amber alerts.
The test will be broadcast on television and radio and delivered to compatible wireless devices connected to an LTE or 5G network.

articles.title: University of Birmingham pauses plans to move Shakespeare Institute after outcry
articles.summary:
Vice-chancellor halts proposed relocation from Stratford-upon-Avon but offers no guarantees over future

The University of Birmingham has paused plans to

blocks.text: The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move its much-loved Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to its city campus after an outcry from scholars, actors and enthusiasts around the world.

Prof Adam Tickell, the university’s vice-chancellor and principal, issued a statement on Tuesday evening saying proposals to relocate the institute and its renowned 60,000-volume library to the university’s Edgbaston campus would be put on hold while its future was explored.

“Over the past few days, we have heard very clearly how much the Shakespeare Institute matters not only to the University of Birmingham but also to Stratford-upon-Avon, to our partners at the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, and to people who love Shakespeare around the world,” Tickell said.

“I have therefore decided to pause the planned move as we explore how and whether the institute can have a vibrant and viable future in Stratford-upon-Avon.” He pointed out that interest in studying in Shakespeare’s home town has been low in recent years and made no promises about the institute’s future.

Prof Michael Dobson, the director of the Shakespeare Institute, who said he would resign if the move went ahead, described the announcement as “a start”, but said he would have preferred the decision to be reversed rather than paused.

blocks.caption: The Shakespeare Institute and the University of Birmingham’s 60,000-volume library were due to be moved to the Edgbaston campus. Photograph: Andrew Fox/The Guardian

blocks.text: The original decision to relocate, announced to devastated institute staff and students last week, was lambasted on social media as “near-philistine”, “unbelievably stupid”, “extraordinarily sad and shortsighted” and “an appalling act of cultural vandalism”.

A petition protesting against the move, led by the actors Samuel West and Dame Janet Suzman, rapidly gathered 15,000 signatures, as supporters of the institute around the world registered their anger at the proposal.
Tickell said: “The university’s commitment to Shakespearean studies has never been in doubt but we need to be honest about the challenges and opportunities the institute faces.

“Interest in studying in Stratford has remained very low for several years. At the same time, we have seen significant growth for related subjects on our Birmingham campus and the thriving creative industries sector in Birmingham creates real opportunities for Shakespearean research and scholarship.
after newsletter promotion

“Over the next six months, we will work with the Shakespeare Institute, the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, and other partners, students, and alumni to ensure that the Shakespeare Institute re-establishes itself at the heart of scholarship, performance and reception for England’s greatest poet in both Birmingham and Stratford-upon-Avon.”
Dobson said: “I look forward to continuing to try to persuade the university management that we can find a viable, permanent future for the institute in Stratford-upon-Avon.”

articles.title: American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody
articles.summary:
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage

A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has…

blocks.text: A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police ‌on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating ⁠to espionage.
The arrest was part of an investigation by UK Counter Terrorism Policing, working with authorities including the US military and the FBI.
The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement on Tuesday: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.
“That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase.

“An army officer is in custody as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London and our partners at UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command. Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action.”
The suspect, a senior soldier, was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, which serves as the headquarters of Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the Guardian understands.
He was arrested on suspicion of offences under section 1 and section 3 of the National Security Act and was in custody at a London police station.
US authorities have said Tyner joined the military in 2008 as a senior human resources officer, and was deployed overseas to Iraq, Qatar and Afghanistan.
He was identified on Friday after British counter-terror police secured more time to question him.
As part of the investigation, officers carried out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said last week.

Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing: said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS [Crown Prosecution Service], who in turn engaged with the attorney general’s office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.
“This decision was made in line with existing international protocols.
“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.
“I’d like to praise the excellent work of the investigation team here in the UK to get us to this point and we will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case “should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the constitution.”
He added: “Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served.
“This effort is a great example of the remarkable partnership Army Counterintelligence Command has with army prosecutors, the FBI, DOJ [Department of Justice], and the UK.”

blocks.text: A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.

CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.

articles.title: Trump nominates Chris LaNeve as army chief after Hegseth fired predecessor
articles.summary:
LaNeve, who served as Hegseth’s senior military commander, nominated to permanently replace Gen Randy George

Donald Trump has nominated Gen Chris LaNeve to be the US army’s top officer,…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has nominated Gen Chris LaNeve to be the US army’s top officer, making permanent his interim service after defense secretary Pete Hegseth unexpectedly fired his predecessor in April.
LaNeve had been serving as Hegseth’s senior military commander before his nomination for a fourth star and service as vice chief of staff of the army in February.

Two months later, Hegseth fired army chief of staff Gen Randy George. While the firing has never been explained, George had insisted on an official investigation into an unauthorized 28 March army helicopter flyover near the Tennessee home of musician Kid Rock, which Hegseth blocked.
LaNeve’s relatively short tenure as a four-star general has raised questions among Democrats and Republicans, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal.

LaNeve, 59, graduated from the University of Arizona in 1990 and later earned master’s degrees from Central Michigan University and the US Army Command and General Staff College. He has served in a wide variety of command roles, including a rotation as the commander of the 82nd Airborne Division and the 8th Army in Korea.

articles.title: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say
articles.summary:
Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents

A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem

blocks.text: A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.

Abu Younis, a cousin of Wadha’s husband, told the Guardian that the violence had begun when a group of settlers attacked a young boy they accused of entering a courtyard seized from its Palestinian residents.

Dozens of Israeli settlers, some of them armed, moved into eight buildings in al-Duyuk al-Tahta two weeks ago with the backing of the settler organisation Nachala and a regional council representing illegal settlements in the central West Bank.
“A vehicle carrying settlers chased him,” Younis said. “There were about 15 settlers in several vehicles. They began firing indiscriminately, killing the woman.”
Witnesses said Palestinian residents began to throw stones to defend themselves, as more settlers arrived at the scene, shooting at civilians and injuring six men.

Wadha’s son, Arafat Fidhat, was wounded after he rushed to the scene after learning that his mother had been shot. His wife, Naama Fidhat, told Reuters he was in shock when he accidentally collided with a parked car belonging to one of the settlers.
Witnesses said the vehicle was empty at the time, but that settlers responded by opening fire, wounding Arafat in the torso.

blocks.caption: Mourners attend the funeral of Wadha Fadha, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman killed by Israeli settlers, near Jericho. Photograph: Jamal Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Naama Fidhat said her husband was being taken to a hospital in Ramallah when Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance and arrested him. She said Israeli soldiers also arrested their son, Wadha’s grandson, early the following morning.
“What did we do? We didn’t do anything,” she said. “This is our house, they were the ones who came with weapons … we were unarmed, we were sleeping.”

The Israeli military said a group of Palestinians in ​a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”. It said the Palestinians exited the vehicle and attacked the Israelis, who opened fire at the Palestinians. “There are Israeli and Palestinian ​casualties in the incident,” the military said.
The arrival of the Israeli settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta had raised fears among Palestinian residents who have faced repeated attacks in the area.

The Binyamin regional council, which covers 47 illegal settlements, claimed the properties in the village had been bought from Palestinians, but Jericho’s governor, Hussein Hamayel, disputed the claim, saying the land belonged to the state and could not legally be sold.
Human rights activists said settlers had assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg during the takeover earlier this month.

“Since the settlers moved into the area on 4 November our lives have been turned upside down,” Younis told the Guardian. “We used to live peacefully and safely on our farms, but since the settlers arrived, our lives have become a living hell. I own 53 dunams [5.3 hectares] of farmland with greenhouses, but we are no longer allowed to access them. We have suffered devastating financial losses, and now people are being killed as well.”

There has been a sharp ​rise in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank, territory Israel captured in the 1967 six-day war. UN bodies and most ​countries deem the settlements illegal, which Israel disputes.

On Tuesday, Suleiman Abu Srour, a photographer for the Palestinian news agency Wafa, was beaten by Israeli soldiers while covering events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta. Wafa said he suffered fractures and bruises, was detained for six hours and had his phone confiscated before being released.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

articles.title: Australia sanctions individuals and company involved in illegal West Bank settlements
articles.summary:
Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong says rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are ‘extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution’

blocks.text: Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on those involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank.
The sanctions will prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to the group.

In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements. The statement did not name the company.
Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the United Kingdom on the sanctions.

“We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions. We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.”
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”

Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
