articles.title: Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone
articles.summary: Milburn lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare

blocks.text: It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone.

What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security.

It is nothing less, Milburn suggests boldly, than rescuing an abandoned generation and giving their lives “shape and meaning”. It is about strategy, planning – making sure all kids are school ready by the age of five, as well as job ready by 18 – but it is also across the finer detail: he asks bosses at one point, for example, if they might at least bother to reply to young people’s job applications.

It is not dull, as employment policy goes: this is Milburn possibly at the peak of his persuasive powers, throwing it all at one last big legacy-defining job, joined by an advisory committee packed with old Blair-era policy comrades. This is not your modest, average independent policy review, he suggests at one stage, but “a broad-based manifesto for change” on a generational scale. It’s not a plan, he says, so much as a 278-page settlement, a recasting of the state, laws, and institutions.
after newsletter promotion

For the most part Milburn is well tuned to Labour voter ears. There are promises of full employment for the young and promises to change the way the labour market operates. There are calls to double the number of youth apprenticeships and roll out a dynamic new cohort of specialist career advisers. There is no shyness about the central role of the state in fixing markets that have let down young people so terribly.

Nor are the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) to blame for their predicament, he concludes. This is not a snowflake generation, lazy and unambitious. Milburn acknowledges the central negative presence in their lives of poverty, inequality, intergenerational unfairness, the scourge of mental ill health and disability discrimination.

Which is why Milburn’s proposed welfare changes lurk like a dark heart. We have been told for months now that this is a government that, unlike its predecessor, does not do “crude cuts”. But this is a plan that proposes a young, out of work disability claimant on a £2,000 benefit income has that replaced with £339 a month. This, it concludes, is better for their longer-term life chances.

For Milburn it is all about the guarantee, the promise of work and training and “the gift of a future”. It’s short-term pain for long-term gain. Not that they have much choice: young people will be expected to work or train. If they don’t engage they will have their benefits sanctioned. The report picks at welfare reform like an itch, obsessively; given half a chance it says it would love to overhaul everyone else’s benefits too. At one point it describes disability benefits as the “weakest link in the chain”. About half of Neets do not claim any benefits at all.

Within 10 years, the plan would strip £3.6bn from young people’s net disability benefits. Past experience, says the poverty charity the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, shows disability benefit cuts deepen poverty, worsen mental health and do not increase the likelihood of finding a job. It is unclear if Labour backbenchers will revolt on benefits as they did last year, but they too may ask themselves why Milburn offers jobs and skills support at the expense of financial security. Why cannot it be both?

articles.title: Using law to try to silence abuse victims is ‘ultimate form of gaslighting’, MPs told
articles.summary:
Woman sued by alleged rapist tells justice committee that Slapp lawsuits present perpetrator as victim of wrongdoing

Attempts by perpetrators and alleged perpetrators of sexual abuse to…

blocks.text: Attempts by perpetrators and alleged perpetrators of sexual abuse to silence their victims using the law are “the ultimate form of gaslighting”, MPs have heard.

Verity Nevitt, a co-founder of the Gemini Project, a survivor-led nonprofit organisation, told the House of Commons justice committee about the ordeal of being sued by the man she and her sister, Lucy, respectively accused of sexual abuse and rape.

At Tuesday’s session, held after the conviction of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault and the allegations of improper behaviour against David Walliams, which he denies, MPs heard that wealthy and powerful men silenced victims through injunctions, non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) and strategic lawsuits against public participation, known as Slapps. The latter are used to harass or intimidate opponents speaking out on matters of public interest.

Nevitt said: “When you experience rape or sexual assault, choice is taken from you, and being subject to a Slapp replicates those dynamics in the sense that you have no choice but to be subject to it … and I think that also means that these cases are quite attractive to someone who is coercive, controlling.

“I think Slapps allow a flipping of the script where the perpetrator is presented as a victim of wrongdoing, and then the victim/survivor is presented as the aggressor by being made a defendant. It’s an egregious reversal of reality, and it’s the ultimate form of gaslighting.”
Nevitt and her sister reported the man to police but, when the case was dropped, they decided to name him on social media to warn others, which led to him suing them.
They eventually reached an out-of-court agreement and, having waived their right to anonymity, the sisters could talk about the case without naming him.

Nevitt told MPs that in the case brought against her and her sister the truth “didn’t matter at all” – it was all about the costs. She said that after the first hearing, the solicitor took the sisters aside and told them they would have to find £100,000 to make it to the next hearing.
Jennifer Robinson, a barrister and co-author of Silenced Women: Why the Law Fails Women and How to Fight Back, told MPs that survivors who were sued faced huge costs.

“The chilling effect is actually much broader than simply women themselves who want to speak out,” she said. “It’s also having a chilling effect on journalists’ willingness and their newspapers’ willingness to report their stories, which is not in the public interest. We can’t tackle violence against women if we can’t talk about it.”
Harriet Wistrich, the chief executive of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said there was a good argument for “very severe cost capping” in such cases.

Rupert Cowper-Coles, a partner and head of media at RPC solicitors, told the committee the UK was a “major outlier amongst western democracies” because it did not have a general anti-Slapp law but one that only covered disclosures relating to economic crime.

Robinson said: “Why are we privileging the protection of public interest speech on economic crimes and not for crimes against women in the context of the crisis of violence against women that we have in society?”

articles.title: Calgary high school says too many students are getting food delivered
articles.summary: A Calgary high school sent parents a memo this week asking them to rein in their children’s increasing use of food delivery apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash during school hours.

image.caption: St. Francis High School sent parents a memo Monday outlining concerns about the "increased use of food delivery apps" by students. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A Calgary high school sent parents a memo this week asking them to rein in their children’s increasing use of food delivery apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash during school hours.
St. Francis asks parents to ask kids to stop ordering food during class time

In the letter, St. Francis High School administrators said while the deliveries may be convenient, they can also be disruptive to classrooms, and pose security risks to have students interacting with individuals they don’t know on school grounds.

“As the safety and security of everyone at St. Francis is our priority, we ask that you please have a conversation with your child and ask them to not use any food delivery services during the instructional time of the day," the letter said.

Lee Martin, who represents Calgary Catholic teachers for the Alberta Teachers’ Association, told CBC News it's become more of an issue in recent years. He heard from one teacher just this week who said a driver tried to deliver food right to a classroom window.
“I think that as public educators we want our children fed,” said Martin. “However, this seems to be a bit out of control.”
A food drop-off cart outside an elementary school in Calgary's southeast. (Submitted by Lee Martin)
And it’s not only at high schools.

At one elementary school, he said upwards of 30 parents were either dropping off food or sending deliveries there daily, so the school set up a table in the foyer where students can go search for their bag at lunchtime.
A spokesperson for the Calgary Catholic School District said to their knowledge, St. Francis is the only school in its board addressing the matter.
In a statement, the Calgary Board of Education said it doesn’t have a specific policy on food deliveries, and it’s up to principals at individual schools to set guidelines if it is an issue.
“Students are discouraged from ordering deliveries into the building, though we are aware they may meet the driver in other locations on school property,” the statement said.
Students say it’s common, not necessarily an issue
Outside St. Francis, delivery driver Ali Nuru dropped off food for a student Tuesday. He says he’ll typically end up doing a couple of school deliveries a week.
“Most of the time I bring from McDonald's,” he said.
Delivery driver Ali Nuru says he typically delivers a couple of times a week to high schools, with McDonald's the No. 1 meal of choice. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)
Students said it’s fairly routine to see classmates meeting drivers in the parking lot to pick up their orders.

“A lot of times — I'm kind of snitching — but they'll be like, ‘oh can I go to the bathroom' and then they just go meet the driver around the school, like the front of the school and then bring the food in with them,” said Grade 11 student Rebira Assefa.
However, she said it hasn’t been a big deal in her classrooms, with most students unbothered by it.
The bathroom excuse can be an issue though, said Grade 11 student Bradley White, since only so many students are allowed out of a class at a time.
“Like if someone's out for too long, then the teacher will be like, ‘OK, no one's allowed to use the bathroom for the rest of class because this person ruined it for everyone,’” said White.
Plus, he said it can be a distraction when someone orders an “excessive” amount of food for themselves and their friends, and brings it into class.
Cracking down on it, though, could be tricky.

“I don't really know how they would enforce a policy where you're not allowed to order something, because kids are going to do it anyways. They'll end up rebelling because you put another policy in,” said Grade 12 student Alysa Utigard.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jennifer is a reporter with CBC Calgary. Previously, she worked for CTV News in Toronto. You can reach her at jennifer.keiller@cbc.ca
With files from Colleen Underwood

articles.title: Milburn calls for tax cuts for businesses hiring young people despite union concerns
articles.summary: Youth unemployment review risks clash with unions and Labour left over workers’ rights and minimum wage

blocks.text: Alan Milburn has called on ministers to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people, setting up a potential clash with trade unions and the Labour left over employment rights.
The former health secretary published the results of his year-long review into youth unemployment on Wednesday, in what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a “watershed moment” for young people.

But while ministers embraced his central recommendation of cutting benefit and sickness payments to pay for more concerted employment support, his recommendations on workers’ rights, national insurance and the minimum wage pose potentially awkward dilemmas for the government.

In the 278-page report, Milburn called for ministers to cut national insurance for companies that hire young workers, to apply a “cautionary principle” when abolishing exploitative zero-hours contracts and to slow the rise in the youth rates of the minimum wage.

“A new bargain needs to be struck between employers and government: employers should create more first chances; government should make it easier and less risky for employers to do so,” he wrote. “That is the give and the get.”

Trade unions warned against some of his proposals, despite broadly welcoming Milburn’s push for a drastic expansion in state support to help the almost 1 million young people not in education or work.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, urged the government to “crack on and deliver its guaranteed hours rights in full” in the face of lobbying from business groups.

blocks.caption: Young people at an employment fair in London. Under Milburn’s plan, the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service. Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The Guardian

blocks.text: “The past decade and a half has tested to destruction the idea that low-paid insecure work is good for our economy and young people’s employment prospects. It’s for the birds,” he said.

Burnham welcomed Milburn’s report on Tuesday, telling cabinet colleagues it represented a “comprehensive vision” for how to change the welfare, health and education systems for young people to help them into work.
He then joined Pat McFadden in the Commons, where the work and pensions secretary told MPs the government would deliver “a new settlement for young people”.

Under Milburn’s plan, the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work.
It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people.

The new system would be paid for largely by replacing young people’s disability and sickness benefits with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably less than some people can currently claim.

People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”.

The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn in higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said.
Ministers and Milburn have worked hard to avoid the response that greeted Keir Starmer’s attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments.
The former prime minister backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably set in motion his eventual departure from office.
Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year’s rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals.
Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review “an opportunity of a generation”, adding: “We must change the status quo.”
after newsletter promotion

But while Burnham and McFadden expressed support for the idea of shifting money from benefits to employment support schemes, they did not explicitly back Milburn’s recommendations on either national insurance contributions or zero-hours contracts.
McFadden told the Commons on Tuesday: “We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward.”

On the minimum wage, Milburn urged ministers to continue applying “caution” when judging how quickly to increase the youth rate, after Labour promised in 2024 to raise it to the same level as the adult rate.
And on banning zero-hours contracts, he warned: “There is a risk that in trying to address a legitimate challenge, the solution has unintended consequences. I believe this is likely to be the case.”

blocks.caption: Banning zero-hours contracts was at the heart of Labour’s election manifesto.  Photograph: Milorad Kravic/Getty Images

blocks.text: Business leaders welcomed the recommendations, in particular the call to backtrack on Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions with a tax cut for under-25s, starting in retail and hospitality.

Maxine Bligh, the interim chief executive of the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, said: “Tackling the Neet [not in education, employment or training] crisis gives ministers the perfect opportunity to reconsider a guaranteed hours gamble that risks costing jobs and damaging the chances of young people accessing the labour market.”
Industry chiefs have intensified their lobbying against the government’s Employment Rights Act, with bosses finding a warm reception from Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said Labour was pressing ahead with an “unemployment act” that would hit youth jobs. “You cannot solve a youth jobs emergency without jobs, and this government has spent two years destroying them.”
Government analysis published this year showed estimated costs to employers could range from £350m to £2.9bn a year, with a central estimate of £1.1bn.
But unions and charities urged Burnham not to water down the plans, arguing that low-paid and insecure work had contributed significantly to Britain’s youth jobs crisis.

Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, said “crucial policies” on workers’ rights needed to be retained. “We are clear that the government must ensure that employment is fairly paid and secure, with workers being treated with dignity and respect.”

Banning zero-hours contracts was a promise at the heart of Labour’s election manifesto. Under Starmer, however, elements of the party’s plan to “make work pay” were watered down amid opposition from business.

Clare McNeil, the chief executive of the charity Timewise, said: “Where we disagree with Alan Milburn is in any suggestion that the new responsibilities in the Employment Rights Bill will stop employers hiring.”

Allies of the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, who had championed the government’s zero-hours plan as Starmer’s deputy, insisted that her proposals would not discourage employers from hiring young people. However, she is no longer in charge of the policy, which must now be implemented by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.

articles.title: U.K. sanctions Israeli companies involved in building illegal settlements in West Bank
articles.summary: Britain said on Tuesday it would impose sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, as part of its effort to protect the idea of a…

image.caption: An Israeli settlement is seen as Israeli military machinery uproots olive trees in the Palestinian village of Beit Rima near Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank on Sept. 24. The U.K. announced new sanctions on Tuesday that would be imposed on eight Israeli construction companies involved involved in

blocks.text: World·New

Britain said on Tuesday it would impose sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, as part of its effort to protect the idea of a two-state solution.
Britain says newly imposed sanctions to disrupt firms' access to finance, support for more construction

Britain said on Tuesday it would impose sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, as well as on an activist group responsible for blocking aid to Gaza.

The firms targeted for asset freezes and director disqualifications include Har Hevron Development Company, Hemdat Shomron and S.A.G. (Velvel) Construction and Development, which build and develop homes in the West Bank.

The government announced the sanctions package shortly before the final deadlines for the E1 tender, a settlement project that would bisect the Israeli-occupied West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem, fragmenting the land that Palestinians hope will form the heart of a state.

"Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach," British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement. "That is why my message on E1 is clear: Do not bid, do not build and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution."

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the sanctions were a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies," adding that the Israeli government would consider new ways to strengthen settlements in the West Bank.

"Israel will respond to the British government’s actions with countermeasures. A wide range of possible responses is currently under consideration. Our decisions will be announced in due course," he said in a post on X.
Israel pushes into West Bank for settlement expansion

Saar remains foreign minister in a caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu. An Oct. 27 election stripped Netanyahu's coalition of its parliamentary majority but no winner emerged, and talks are ongoing to form a new government.
The Palestinian Authority welcomed the British sanctions and called for other countries to take similar action.
Deteriorated U.K.-Israel relationship
The sanctions are the latest in a series of measures by Britain targeting the settlement policy and underscore Israel's growing diplomatic isolation among some traditional allies.

Britain's relationship with Israel has deteriorated significantly over the past three years because of disagreements over the way that Israel has conducted its war against Hamas and the Israeli government's plans to expand settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Israel in September threatened to close the British Consulate building in East Jerusalem in response to London’s decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
British and Israeli diplomats last month reached a last-minute agreement to avoid the closure of the consulate.
Palestinian farmers risk their lives to pick their olives

Britain joined several other countries including Canada in 2025 in recognizing a Palestinian state as a means of advancing the two-state solution, and in September announced plans to block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

Last year, Britain also imposed sanctions on two far-right Israeli cabinet ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, accusing them of repeatedly inciting violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.

While those measures were co-ordinated with international partners, Britain acted alone on Tuesday in sanctioning the Israeli companies, saying the move would disrupt their access to finance and support for further construction in the West Bank.
Israeli group obstructing Gaza aid sanctioned

As part of the measures announced on Tuesday, the government also imposed sanctions on Tzav 9, an Israeli activist group that it said had regularly blocked humanitarian aid trucks delivering food, water and fuel to the Gaza Strip. The new sanctions placed include an asset freeze and director disqualification, which prevent sanctioned individuals from using corporate structures to operate or raise funds.

In June 2024, the U.S. State Department under the Biden administration sanctioned Tzav 9, which it described as a "violent extremist Israeli group." The European Union followed suit a month later by also imposing sanctions on the group under its Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime.

According to the United Nations, over 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins that humanitarian partners and donors purchased are outside Gaza, ready to go in, but are being held by the Israeli authorities, the U.K. said in its statement, adding that the Israeli authorities also continue to block timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza.

"We are suffering a lot here in Gaza because of the lack of tents and the lack of sheltering equipment that the Israelis are putting restrictions on," Mohammed Salha, general director of the Palestinian NGO Network in Gaza, told CBC News on Tuesday.
Israel's military agency that co-ordinates aid, COGAT, says it has a proactive "winterization plan" and that supplies and medicines continue to enter Gaza.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Meet the 2027 Grammy best new artist nominees
articles.summary: The 2027 Grammy nominees for best new artist dropped Monday, putting a spotlight on who's reshaping the music scene. If you want to keep your playlist fresh — or at least know what everyone in the…

image.caption: The 2027 Grammy nominees for Best New Artist dropped Monday, putting a spotlight on who's reshaping the music scene. Clockwise from top left: Remi Wolf, Ella Langley, Slayyyter, Geese, Don Toliver, Angine de Poitrine, Sienna Spiro, The Womack Sisters. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Jason Kempin/Emma McIntyre/Gre

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The 2027 Grammy nominees for best new artist dropped Monday, putting a spotlight on who's reshaping the music scene. If you want to keep your playlist fresh — or at least know what everyone in the group chat is talking about — here are the names shaping the conversation.
Not familiar with their music? Don't worry, we've got you covered
The 2027 Grammy nominees for best new artist dropped Monday, putting a spotlight on who's reshaping the music scene.

Despite what the name suggests, a nominee doesn't actually have to be brand new to qualify. Some might even argue "breakthrough artist" would be a better fit for the nominees. With new rules allowing artists to be submitted up to four times instead of three, this year gave both artists putting in the work for years as well as some fresh faces their moment.
Past winners have gone on to become global icons, such as Christina Aguilera, Adele and Billie Eilish. And recent recipients include Olivia Rodrigo, Chappell Roan and Olivia Dean.
So if you want to keep your playlist fresh — or at least know what everyone in the group chat is talking about — here are the names shaping the conversation.
Angine de Poitrine

The Quebec alien-like math rock duo that went from underground favourites to international sensations, seemingly overnight. From Saguenay, Que., the masked, polka-dot-costumed performers build their microtonal sound live with looping pedals while wearing oversized papier mâché heads. The two started 2026 under the radar and have since performed with Shania Twain and opened for Jack White. The anonymous duo — known as Khn and Klek de Poitrine — also picked up three other Grammy nominations on Monday, including best rock performance, best rock album and best alternative music performance.
The hit you might know: Fabienk.
Don Toliver

You may know him from his breakout 2018 feature Can't Say on Travis Scott's ASTROWORLD. The Houston, Texas born rapper has been releasing music for over a decade. Known for his psychedelic trap/R&B sound, he's collaborated with artists ranging from SZA, Baby Keem, Kali Uchis, Kaytranada and Drake. If there was a big rap release, he probably had a hand in it. Toliver is the leading hip-hop artist at this year's Grammys with five nominations for his album Octane and hit single E85.
The hit you might know: E85.
Ella Langley

It's been a huge year for the 27-year-old artist from Alabama. Her breakout hit Choosin' Texas holds the record for longest-running No. 1 in Billboard Hot 100 history. Langley scored seven nominations for that hit and her sophomore album Dandelion. Plus, she's the first country artist since Bobbie Gentry in 1968 to be nominated in each of the big four Grammy awards (album of the year, record of the year, song of the year and best new artist) in a single year, according to Billboard.
The hit you might know: Choosin’ Texas.
Geese

A Brooklyn-based rock quartet fronted by singer/guitarist Cameron Winter, who's also a critically acclaimed solo artist. Geese formed in 2016 and is known for its experimental punk sound, often compared to acts like the Strokes and the Velvet Underground. The group earned a bunch of coverage earlier this year for its marketing team's efforts. Oh, and according to fans, Geese's Saturday Night Live performance of Trinidad is one to watch. The group is up for five trophies, including for the songs Trinidad and Au Pays du Cocaine, as well as their album Getting Killed.
The hit you might know: Au Pays du Cocaine.
Remi Wolf

Remi Wolf isn't your typical pop star — the California artist is known for her high energy and funky basslines, carving out her own lane of soul-infused pop. She actually competed on American Idol in 2014 as a high school senior and broke through with her 2020 EP I'm Allergic to Dogs! Pulling in millions of streams and performing on massive festival and arena stages, she's constantly reinventing herself. And her latest work, Mud, leans a bit more into an indie rock sound.
The hit you might know: Photo ID.
Sienna Spiro

Sienna Spiro has that soulful James Bond theme song sound. She leans into a soulful, jazzy vintage sound in the vein of Adele and Amy Winehouse. The London-based singer-songwriter started posting videos of covers on TikTok in 2021, catching the eyes of major labels before releasing her debut single Need Me in 2024. It was her hit single Die on This Hill that really put her on the map.
The hit you might know: Die on This Hill.
Slayyyter

Take electric dance pop music, cover it in sequins, glitter and a whole lot of gloss, and then throw in a heavy rock edge — that’s what Slayyyter is all about. Her most recent album leans into the early-2000s indie sleaze sound — though she nearly walked away from the industry entirely before making it. Instead of quitting, she put those frustrations into this new record, earning her four Grammy nominations, including best dance/electronic album and recording, as well as best dance pop recording.
The hit you might know: DANCE...
The Womack Sisters

Big stages run in the family for Zeimani, Zekkujcha (Kucha) and Zekuumba (BG) Womack. Their family tree says it all: daughters of Linda and Cecil Womack (of Womack & Womack), nieces of R&B icon Bobby Womack and grandchildren of the legendary Sam Cooke. After spending over a decade performing as backing vocalists for artists like Solange Knowles and releasing music independently, the trio signed to a label in 2025. They followed it with their breakthrough, self-titled debut album, rooted in classic soul and R&B.
The hit you might know: If I Let You.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: Fossil-fuel industry accused of violating Colorado law over not disclosing drilling chemicals
articles.summary:
Non-profit FracTracker Alliance alleges regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling despite 2022 law

The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which…

blocks.text: The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it uses in drilling, a new analysis by the FracTracker Alliance non-profit alleges, and state records show it has used illegal or dangerous compounds while fracking.

Drilling chemicals can include xylene, toluene, benzene, Pfas and other dangerous toxicants, industry records and literature from other regions show. A first-in-the-nation 2022 Colorado law requires fossil-fuel operators and their suppliers to make public all chemicals used in “downhole oil and gas production”. But regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling, claiming that drilling is not part of production.
FracTracker contends this exemption contradicts the widely held definition of production, including that implied in Colorado’s regulatory literature.

Legislators who authored the law, public health groups, and industry all use definitions of “production” that includes drilling, FracTracker states, and it notes the law requires “disclosure of all chemicals used underground or ‘downhole’ in oil and gas wells”.

Meanwhile, at least five chemicals that were reported for use in fracking are prohibited by Colorado law, FracTracker alleges. It also found fossil-fuel companies reported using at least three highly toxic chemicals that raise serious safety questions.
About 43,000 people live within a mile of the state’s wells, and many within a few hundred feet. Regulators are flying blind on what the sum impact of the chemicals may be, the authors allege.

“This is a public health crisis and it should be treated as such,” Shannon Smith, FracTracker’s executive director, told the Guardian. FracTacker is a non-profit that investigates and monitors public health threats created by the fossil-fuel industry, and advocates for protections. It began in Pennsylvania in 2010, but now organizes nationally.

Fracking operators and their suppliers are supposed to disclose all downhole chemical ingredients to the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC) regulatory agency within 150 days. The agency then must post the chemicals on its website.

blocks.caption: Birds fly past an oil and gas rig in Weld county, south of Greeley, Colorado, in November 2022. Photograph: RJ Sangosti/The Denver Post via Getty Images

blocks.text: ECMC literature implies the agency considers drilling as part of oil and gas production. In a statement, an ECMC spokesperson said the agency was “aware of differing views regarding the scope and implementation of the chemical disclosure requirements”.

“We are applying the law and Commission rules under the current statutory and regulatory framework while continuing to work with stakeholders to clarify these issues and support consistent, appropriate implementation,” the spokesperson said.
Halliburton, Chevron and Occidental Petroleum are among the state’s top fossil-fuel producers.
In a statement, a Chevron spokesperson said the company “is committed to safe and responsible operations in Colorado”.
“We take chemical-disclosure requirements seriously and remain focused on meeting our obligations and maintaining transparent, responsible operating practices,” the spokesperson added.

In order to drill wells and extract minerals, fossil-fuel operators pump huge volumes of pressurized liquid into the earth to fracture – or “frack” – bedrock, stimulating the release of trapped oil and gas. These fluids are mostly water and sand by volume, but they also contain industrial chemicals, including biocides, surfactants and lubricants.

Hundreds of studies have pointed to health risks for those in fracking regions. Toxic chemicals such as formaldehyde, Pfas and benzene have been widely detected or reported in fracking fluids. These and other chemicals used – or thought to be used – in production are linked to issues such as cancer, hormone disruption and neurological damage.

Gas companies reported as many as 11 spills a week in 2018, and people are exposed to the chemicals through multiple pathways, including groundwater, above ground spills, wastewater seepage into drinking water supplies, and air emissions.
The ECMC has told FracTracker that it does not consider drilling to be part of the fracking and production said the report’s author, Dusty Horwitt, FracTracker’s senior research and policy counsel.

“That was news to us, and it is not consistent with The American Petroleum Institute definition of what oil and gas production is,” Horwitt added. API literature shows oil and gas production includes “drilling, extraction, and recovery of oil from underground”.

Meg Froelich, the Colorado state representative who co-wrote the 2022 legislation, said she intended for drilling chemicals to be disclosed. The legislation is called “Concerning enhanced oversight of the chemicals used in oil and gas production.” Production includes drilling, Froelich said.
She accused the ECMC of “word-parsing” and added that she was “mad about their stalling”.
“The law covers everything that goes downhole because everything that goes downhole has the potential to affect neighbors,” Froelich told the Guardian.

The ECMC until recent years has largely worked to promote the fossil-fuel industry, and only since Democrats took over the state government has it shifted to also protect public health, but the shift has come in “fits and starts”, Froelich said.

State records show that wells covered by law operated without drilling chemical disclosure for at least a collective 843,369 days from the rules’ implementation to May 16, when the analysis was conducted.
The law also requires fossil-fuel companies to provide schools, first responders and other community institutions with lists of chemicals it uses, but it has failed to do that, advocates say.

The report comes after a previous analysis reported on by the Guardian found Colorado fossil-fuel companies pumped at least 30m lb of secret chemicals into the ground over an 18-month period without making legally required disclosures. Out of over 1,100 fracked sites across the state, companies did not disclose 675, or about 60%.

blocks.caption: An oilfield worker walks past an open door at a drill pad in Windsor, Colorado. Photograph: RJ Sangosti/The Denver Post via Getty Images

blocks.text: Since then, the compliance rate is closer to 100% – except for the drilling chemicals, advocates say.

The report raises questions about which chemicals are being used for drilling. A recent law banned any use of Pfas at oil and gas sites, and industry literature and peer-reviewed research suggests that Pfas are a common drilling chemical. Horwitt told the Guardian he fears the chemicals may be used in Colorado.

“Publications, including those issued by major oil and gas-producing nations Canada and Norway, report that PFAS is used for multiple purposes in oil and gas production including drilling and enhanced oil recovery,” FracTracker states. The lack of drilling chemical disclosure in Colorado “creates uncertainty about whether companies are complying with the PFAS ban”, the report added.
Meanwhile, records from Ohio show the frequent use of xylene, the report states. The chemical can cause headaches, dizziness, confusion, loss of muscle coordination, and, in high doses, death.

FracTracker also points to five chemicals that were disclosed as being used for fracking on some well pads despite state rules prohibiting their use in fracking: 1-butanol, 2-butoxyethanol, 1,4-dioxane, N,N-dimethylformamide and BMPA. Some of these compounds are linked to cancer, liver disease, and harm to developing children.
In its statement, the ECMC said it had “issued notices of alleged violation when prohibited substances are identified, including cases involving 1-butanol, 2-butoxyethanol and 1,4-dioxane”.

Among potentially harmful chemicals that are permitted are acrylamide, ethylene oxide and methanol. FracTracker noted that those were among the chemicals disclosed as being used in a well in Galeton that sprayed a geyser of gas and at least 3.7m gallons of fluid for over four days in April 2025.

Living near wells has well-established links to leukemia, birth abnormalities and other serious health problems. Residents in July reported to the Guardian that they are plagued by loud noise, acrid air emissions, headaches, nosebleeds and respiratory issues.

articles.title: National Security Agency network for internal communications goes down
articles.summary:
NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails

The National Security Agency’s classified internal communications…

blocks.text: The National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network went down on Tuesday, disrupting work at the US signals intelligence agency, according to several US media reports.

The network, known as NSANet, is used by NSA staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence. The New York Times and CNN reported that the agency had told staff at its Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters to arrive in staggered shifts while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily.
The NSA did not respond to a request for comment.

The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said.

Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff.

A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong.

The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights, a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services. None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible.
Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.”
He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe.

Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions.
Shrai Popat contributed reporting

articles.title: Convicted rapist Russell Brand under investigation for claiming innocence from behind bars
articles.summary: The Ministry of Justice in the U.K. is investigating whether comedian and convicted rapist Russell Brand is guilty of breaking prison rules after his wife shared a message from Brand on his YouTube…

image.caption: Comedian and actor Russell Brand, seen here accompanied by his wife Laura Brand at Southwark Crown Court in London earlier this month, is being investigated by British authorities for breaking prison rules about making public statements. (Thomas Krych/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The Ministry of Justice in the U.K. is investigating whether comedian and convicted rapist Russell Brand is guilty of breaking prison rules after his wife shared a message from Brand on his YouTube channel claiming his innocence.
Brand's wife read his statement to his millions of YouTube subscribers on Sunday

The Ministry of Justice in the U.K. is investigating whether comedian and convicted rapist Russell Brand broke prison rules about public statements after his wife shared a message from Brand on his YouTube channel claiming his innocence.

"I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening," said his wife Laura Brand, saying she was reading a note from Brand from prison to his 6.6 million subscribers.
In the U.K., prisoners are banned from making statements that could cause distress to victims. Breaking that rule could result in Brand receiving an extended sentence or losing privileges.
Brand, 51, is currently serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assault.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesperson called the statement "appalling," and said it is being "urgently investigated."
"Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress ​to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances," the spokesperson said.
Brand, seen here leaving Southwark Crown Court in London earlier this month, was convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault. (Alastair Grant/The Associated Press)
The spokesperson added that prisoners could not ​get around the rules by asking another person to read their comments.
U.K. Justice Secretary Alex Norris posted about the statement from Brand on X, saying, "I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules."
Possible sentence increase
The statement came at the 54-minute mark of the couple's weekly podcast episode, part of which was pre-recorded.
"Russell has asked me to read something to you today," said Laura Brand, followed by the claim of innocence from her husband.

If he is found to have broken the rules, Brand could face restrictions on social visits and communication, or lose privileges such as access to time in the gym or TV. It could also result in an extension of his prison sentence.
Laura Brand, seen here arriving at Southwark Crown Court in London earlier this month, shared Brand's statement on the couple's weekly podcast. (Kin Cheung/The Associated Press)

Brand rose to prominence in the 2000s as a comedian, broadcaster and Hollywood star, starring in movies such as Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and working for MTV, BBC and Channel Four. He has since turned to YouTube, where he's made a name for himself as an evangelical influencer and right-wing conspiracy theorist.
Brand was accused by an additional six women of sexual misconduct last week, following his conviction.
He has already been convicted of a rape dating back to 2009, as well as three sexual assaults. He was sentenced to nine years in prison for the rape, and 35 months in prison for the sexual assaults.
Brand has denied the accusations, and claimed he has never had non-consensual sex.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Deutsche Bank under fire after internal documents made public
articles.summary: A cache of internal records outlines the bank's dealings with Jeffrey Epstein, Donald Trump and Russian oligarchs. The German lender has sought to deflect criticism by claiming its bad behavior is a…

image.caption: Dark days ahead for Germany's biggest lender? Deutsche Bank shares plunged on Tuesday after the publication of damning internal documentsImage: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP

blocks.text: Deutsche Bank is in damage control mode again after an international consortium of more than 200 investigative journalists published internal documents from the global lender on Tuesday under the name "Inside Deutsche Bank."

The documents, published in Der Spiegel, Financial Times, Le Monde and The New York Times, among others, cover Deutsche Bank's business dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, now US President Donald Trump, and a host of Russian oligarchs.

Gleaned from nearly 15 million documents leaked to a journalist from India and another from South Africa, the e-mails and meeting minutes trace the bank's aggressive pursuit of business deals in Russia, and with high-profile Russian oligarchs, right up until Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — despite risk warnings from numerous managers.

Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing was among the executives who took part in the bank's Russia strategy working group. The bank also still employs more than 160 people in Russia and generated 2025 pre-tax profits of €61 million ($67 million) there through a local subsidiary.
Money laundering, oligarchs, terrorists: How corrupt are the banks?
Not just about Deutsche Bank's business with Trump, Epstein and Russians

In all, the documents cover the past 20 years of the German lender's business dealings and raise questions about the efficacy of internal controls by showing that Deutsche Bank had repeatedly put financial interests before international sanctions compliance and anti-money laundering rules.

Other red flags raised in Tuesday's reports suggest that Deutsche Bank sought to set up tax-optimization schemes for wealthy clients, that criminal networks may have been able to move illicit cash through the institution, that it helped facilitate arms deals, that it helped companies in environmentally damaging industries and that it held funds for the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Has Deutsche Bank really changed its ways?

Beyond more recent negative headlines involving alleged anti-money laundering and compliance failures, Deutsche Bank has been trying to restore its public image ever since its involvement in the US subprime mortgage rate scandal helped trigger the 2008 global financial crisis — a fiasco that ultimately cost the bank more than €20 billion in penalties and settlements.

When Sewing later took over in 2018, he promised to turn the institution around. Although he has made Deutsche Bank profitable once again, he did so at the cost of massive job cuts, and some compliance failings have continued.
Sewing to the German business daily Handelsblatt that some mistakes had been made under his leadership.

"When you look at the events today, you naturally ask yourself whether you could have done some things differently," he told the paper. "I am not without mistakes," he said, but added that the course he set for the bank "has always been right and remains so."
The bank's shares fell by up to 6% in Tuesday trading.
German government wants 'full transparency' from Deutsche Bank
Deutsche Bank issued a statement claiming that the reports were old news and that the institution had long ago turned over a new leaf.

In an e-mailed statement to the press, Deutsche Bank Supervisory Board Chairman Alexander Wynaendts wrote, "During my tenure I haven't seen a single decision from Christian Sewing that I was not comfortable with."
A Tuesday statement from the bank described the revelations as "legacy" matters and claimed they would have no lasting negative financial impact on the institution.

Nevertheless, German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Tuesday called on Deutsche Bank to "provide full transparency regarding how it has addressed past failures and internal control deficiencies and how it will effectively prevent these in the future."
Further, Klingbeil said authorities must investigate and "take necessary action" where appropriate.
'Still easy to avoid regulatory checks'

articles.title: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
articles.summary: The Prince and Princess of Wales were joined by sporting and acting stars for the annual environmental awards ceremony.

blocks.text: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

articles.title: Who to watch in Spain's election race
articles.summary: Spain votes on 29 November, with the conservatives and the far right favourites to win after eight years of Socialist-led rule.

blocks.text: Sánchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.
He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his sixth in 11 years - could be his toughest yet.
Sánchez called the snap election eight months early, seeking to focus on resolving Spain's housing crisis, and vowing "an epic comeback of a progressive Spain" at the ballot box.

But he and his party have been embroiled in a series of corruption scandals, a migrant crisis in Spain's Ceuta exclave on the Moroccan border and two deadly rail disasters nine months apart. The most recent tragedy claimed 69 lives at Urda on 28 October and overshadowed the start of the campaign.
The Socialist leader has been written off in politics before, only to stage comebacks, notably in 2017 and 2023.
He can point to a projected 2.6% annual growth in the Spanish economy in 2026, fuelled by tourism, but the graft cases against his inner circle and family are not going away.

José Luis Ábalos, who was transport minister in Sánchez's government, is now serving a 24-year prison sentence for accepting kickbacks, meanwhile leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.

Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, faces trial over allegations of influence peddling and embezzlement while his brother, David Sánchez, has been banned from public office for nine years for misconduct. Both deny doing anything wrong.
In a defiant message, Begoña Gómez made her first party speech at the Socialist campaign launch, calling for the backing of Spanish women, "because when women step forward, all of Spain follows".
Sánchez's fate could be sealed by the rise of Abascal's anti-immigration, populist Vox - with opinion polls putting them in a comfortable third place and taking votes from the Socialists.

Abascal, 50, denies his party is far-right and has succeeded in bringing Vox into the mainstream, attracting record ratings on one of Spanish state TV's primetime entertainment shows during the campaign.

Repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain are big themes for Abascal, who has accused Pedro Sánchez of promoting an "act of invasion" with his policies.
He has promised to use the Spanish navy to defend the national borders and "send a message to the world that there is no room here for all of Africa and all of the Americas".
The Vox leader joined the PP aged 18, becoming a local councillor first and then an MP in the Basque regional parliament.

His political trajectory was closely shaped by his family's experience of threats and intimidation by Basque militant group Eta. Both his father and grandfather, who held public office, were targeted because of their political roles.

He left the conservatives in 2013, founding Vox the following year and becoming a Spanish MP in 2019, when Vox became the first hard-right party in decades to establish a significant presence in Congress.
Vox has adopted the Trump-inspired slogan "Make Spain Great Again" and advocates a strongly centralised vision of the country strongly opposed to the independence movement in Catalonia.
Critics have described the party's ideology as reminiscent of aspects of the era of dictator Francisco Franco era, which Vox rejects.

Isabel Díaz Ayuso, 48, has been president of the Madrid region since 2019 and has become one of the most influential figures within the People's Party. She leads one of the PP's strongest electoral bastions, with conservatives having ruled the region for the past 31 years.

Ayuso has built a distinct political profile that often sets her apart from the party establishment. Her direct communication style and informal use of language have helped her connect with voters and attract significant media attention.
Her tenure has not been without controversy. Her partner has been the subject of a judicial investigation relating to alleged tax offences and document forgery, allegations he denies.

Opposition parties have also questioned the Madrid regional government's purchase of a luxury penthouse for official use. Critics have challenged the rationale behind the acquisition, while regional authorities have maintained that it was intended as a government workspace.

Socialist Carlos Cuerpo, 46, was chosen by Pedro Sánchez to take charge as interim transport minister after the Urda rail disaster and has become key to his election team. Cuerpo climbed the ranks through the economy ministry and became minister of economy, trade and business in 2023.

He has been ranked as best-regarded politician among the Spanish public, according to the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), and, when asked about his political ambitions has called himself "a team player, and I am committed to the team".
In the same light, Sánchez has said: "I believe politics is a team sport; on the opposing team we have Feijóo and Abascal, and on my team we have Carlos Cuerpo."

Catalonia's Socialist president Salvador Illa is also one to watch. He served as Spain's health minister during the Covid pandemic and some have viewed him as a potential successor as Socialist leader, even though he has backed Sánchez to remain as leader.

Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional…

blocks.text: Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, who chair the committees, said in a press release. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”

The three congressmen chair the foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the intelligence committee of the House of Representatives, respectively. On 12 November, they had signed a letter warning Huang that he could face a subpoena if he did not agree to the closed-door meeting.
Nvidia chips are key to powering the artificial intelligence boom. The Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after allegations of extramarital relationships with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees surfaced.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been Megaspeed International’s executive director. The Singapore-based cloud computing company has bought nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. The company said Alice Huang stepped down in 2025.

Megaspeed ultimately facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of US export controls. On Friday, Malaysia stated that they were investigating whether the company diverted advanced AI ships to other countries.

A recent joint Department of Commerce and Department of Justice letter, stated that the Department of Commerce, under Secretary Howard Lutnick, first started an investigation in Megaspeed on 2024 for potential export control violations. The justice department, led by Attorney General Todd Blanche, took over in 2025.

In his first remarks since his resignation, Jensen Huang said on Thursday he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley tech giants, along with 165,000 signatories to an open letter, have called for his reinstatement. Trump has also signaled his openness for the disgraced tech CEO’s return.
