articles.title: Andy Burnham delays taking stock of UK’s relationship with EU
articles.summary: PM to wait until after Brussels summit at which he hopes for agreements on food, farming and emissions

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer term relationship with the EU, as he comes under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink.

The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels at which he hopes to secure agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

In an interview with Sky News, Burnham admitted that he would now not set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until December – but denied he was “stepping back” from his previous commitments to pursue ties.

The prime minister had been expected to give a speech or deliver a statement setting out options for a closer relationship early next week, probably Monday, and to argue that it would be in the UK’s long-term interest.

While he may still address MPs, he is now likely to focus on the details of the deal secured at the summit, delaying his bigger plans to around the same time as his 10-year plan for the country, No 10 sources said, adding that the two were linked.

No 10 insiders told the Guardian that Burnham wants to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion, with even some Remain-minded MPs acknowledging there is more work to be done.

These will include discussions with European counterparts to establish what the EU is willing to negotiate and whether it might be possible to get a better bespoke deal, or what the terms of rejoining the single market or customs union might be.

Since Burnham announced in September that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he has reiterated that the existing deal is not good enough, and that he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship this autumn.

In addition to the customs union or single market, these could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, reversing Brexit in its entirety, or no change at all.

But after revealing his personal preference would be to fully rejoin the bloc, Burnham has encountered some resistance, including from within the cabinet, with some MPs with Leave-voting seats anxious about reopening the debate.

Senior government figures say that Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be confirmatory after MPs had endorsed a deal.

In his interview, Burnham said: “All I’m going to do is look at what options might be available. And so that people can see the pros and cons, we’ll set those out in due course. There’s no rush to do that. The British public will be in charge of whatever comes next.
“We’ll see how [Friday’s summit] goes. And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.”
The prime minister denied that he was “jumping the gun” or “making any assumptions” about where the UK would end up – but pointed to polling which shows the public wants closer ties with the bloc.
Some Labour MPs, however, are concerned about the impact of freedom of movement in particular, as the debate around immigration in the UK has grown with the rise of Reform UK.
“I won’t get ahead of public opinion. I will listen to what the public feel is the right long term solution,” Burnham added.
While much of the deal expected to be agreed in Brussels on Friday is over the line, there are still tensions over the level of the cap on the youth mobility scheme cap, as well as over tuition fees.

Officials are also expected to discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €50bn (£40bn) safe defence fund, collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and mutual recognition of qualifications.

articles.title: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media during Israel’s election, report finds
articles.summary:
Digital monitors recorded 400% rise in posts attacking Arab Israelis, including Netanyahu’s disproven fraud allegations

Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the…

blocks.text: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the country’s general election last month, digital monitors have said, as politicians including Benjamin Netanyahu levelled disproven allegations against Arab Israeli parties of election fraud.

A new report by the Israel-based Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter recorded a deluge of anti-Arab discourse across social media platforms such as X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in the days surrounding Israel’s 27 October election.
According to FakeReporter’s analysis, anti-Arab sentiment on X rose by more than 400% from election day on 27 October to 29 October. Similar content also spread across Facebook and other platforms.

Arab-majority parties won 19 seats in the Israeli Knesset in last month’s election, potentially putting them in a kingmaker position. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been invited to try to put together a coalition to replace Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist government.

The posts mainly pushed three messages, the first of which was the allegation that “the Arabs stole the election” via fraud, vote buying and foreign interference, according to the report. Israel’s electoral commission had already publicly refuted such claims.
Posts also depicted Arab citizens of Israel as a security threat and called for them to have their right to vote restricted.

Some of the most-viewed posts also came from top Israeli officials and Netanyahu’s post “They stole the election in Israel!” was viewed 1.2m times. A post by the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, calling for heads of Arab political parties was also viewed more than 350,000 times.

FakeReporter said much of the anti-Arab hate speech was fuelled by politicians from Netanyahu’s political bloc. “It can be said that they were a major factor in spreading hate speech against Arab citizens of Israel following the election,” its analysis said.

Arab citizens of Israel, the majority of whom are Palestinians, make up 21% of the population of Israel. Since the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, Arab political leaders have faced increasingly inflammatory attacks and accusations of dual loyalties.

In the run-up to the election, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the country’s two main Arab majority political lists from running – a move later struck down by the Israeli supreme court.
Eisenkot last week condemned what he called a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens.

The Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter sent letters to Google, Meta, TikTok and X on 4 November calling on them to take steps to stop the proliferation of hate speech against Arab citizens of Israel on their platforms.

Only Google responded, saying that Israel’s election is a “Priority 0” for the company and that it has dedicated resources to monitoring traffic around the election, but that the Central Elections Committee had made no requests for extra moderation procedures.

articles.title: Hamilton police investigate after witnesses report group shouting pro-Nazi comments at demonstration
articles.summary: Hamilton police are investigating after receiving reports that a group of about 20 to 25 people dressed in black and wearing masks were shouting pro-Nazi comments at a downtown demonstration Saturday.

image.caption: Police are seeking information, photos and videos after receiving complaints about a weekend demonstration in downtown Hamilton, saying police 'take hate-motivated incidents seriously.' (Hamilton Police Service)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Hamilton police are investigating after receiving reports that a group of about 20 to 25 people dressed in black and wearing masks were shouting pro-Nazi comments at a downtown demonstration Saturday.
'Hate, racism and intimidation have no place in our community,' mayor-elect says

Hamilton police are investigating after receiving reports that a group of about 20 to 25 people dressed in black and wearing masks were shouting pro-Nazi comments at a downtown demonstration on the weekend.
The gathering took place shortly before 6 p.m. ET on Saturday at the corner of King and James streets, police said in a Saturday release.
Witnesses reported seeing participants carrying signs that displayed the words "white only," and hearing the group yell white nationalist and pro-Nazi comments, police said
Police said the group walked south through the Frank A. Cooke Transit Terminal on MacNab Street South before returning to vehicles and leaving the area.

items: Hamilton police seek suspect after neo-Nazi, anti-Black stickers placed on East Hamilton building

blocks.text: "Hamilton police take hate-motivated incidents seriously and remain committed to addressing hate, supporting those impacted, and working alongside community partners to foster a safe and inclusive city," the release said.

Police encourage anyone who experienced or witnessed a hate-motivated crime or incident to report it to help investigators "identify patterns and better understand the experiences of affected communities." This includes incidents that "may not meet the threshold of a criminal offence."
Anyone with information, photos or video footage of Saturday's demonstration, or who witnessed potential criminal activity, is asked to contact Hamilton police.
'Get out of our city,' mayor says

An Instagram post from the Hamilton Anti-Racism Resource Centre (HARRC) shows a video that appears to be a demonstration of about 20 people covered all in black. Some are holding a sign that says "Whites First."
The video was shot at around 5:30 p.m. at the corner of King and James Streets on Saturday, according to centre.
In an email to CBC Hamilton, mayor-elect Keanin Loomis condemned the demonstration, calling it a "disgusting display of hate and white supremacy."
"You are not welcome in Hamilton. Get out of our city," Loomis said. "Hate, racism and intimidation have no place in our community."
He said he is in contact with Hamilton police Chief Frank Bergen as officers work to identify those responsible.
"Hamilton belongs to everyone," Loomis said. "We will not stand by while hate tries to find a home here."

items: Hamilton anti-racism groups give tips on how to avoid unwittingly renting venues to groups deemed extremist

blocks.text: Ward 2 Coun. Cameron Kroetsch said he has spoken with many residents concerned about what ongoing demonstrations by white supremacists in the ward.
"Everyone I know wants them to stop," Kroetsch said in an email to CBC Hamilton, adding that he and other downtown residents see the demonstrations as "disgusting."
He said the use of "white only" messaging is hate speech and said the frequency of such public gatherings is increasing.
Kroetsch said a motion he brought forward during the previous council term will help the city name and condemn such incidents. But he said stronger police action is needed to put a halt to them.
"Until police are willing to respond to this hate in our community, quickly and decisively, it will persist."
Kroetsch noted Saturday's demonstration took place across the street from a police station in Jackson Square and only a few blocks from the main downtown police station.
"We deserve better and I hope the new chief will make this a priority."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeffery is a reporter with CBC Hamilton. He previously worked as a reporter at CBC Saskatchewan in Regina, and was an associate producer at CBC Toronto. You can reach him at jeffery.tram@cbc.ca.

articles.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.summary:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea

At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier…

blocks.text: At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – around 500km to the south.

blocks.caption: The Ukrainian drone that was involved in the latest attack on Kerch bridge. Writing in Cyrilic says: ‘We will stand, Moscow will fall.’ Photograph: “Leon”/Magyar’s Birds

blocks.text: Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.

“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces. Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.

Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.

blocks.caption: President Putin speaks with workers as he inspects the road section of the Kerch bridge in 2018.  Photograph: Alexei Nikolsky/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP

blocks.text: Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine, by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.

As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.

blocks.caption: A satellite image of the Kerch bridge. Photograph: Vantor/Reuters

blocks.text: Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph). SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue. On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.

Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.

A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.

Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight, with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.

blocks.caption: A drone view of what appears to be smoke rising and explosions at the Kerch bridge. Photograph: Security Service Of Ukraine/Reuters

blocks.text: One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”

blocks.caption: A grab taken from a video released by the Ukrainian security service showing damage to the bridge. Photograph: Telegram/@V_Zelensky_official/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.

Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.

“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.

The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

articles.title: Ukraine cripples Crimean bridge in blow to Putin before meeting with Xi, Trump
articles.summary: Ukrainian drones and missiles destroyed the central road section of the bridge linking Russia and Crimea on Tuesday, inflicting a military and symbolic blow on Russian President Vladimir Putin two…

image.caption: A satellite image shows a closeup view of the bridge over the Kerch Strait linking Russia and Crimea that was hit by Ukrainian drones on Monday. (Vantor/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Ukrainian drones and missiles destroyed the central road section of the bridge linking Russia and Crimea on Tuesday, inflicting a military and symbolic blow on Russian President Vladimir Putin two days before he is due to meet the leaders of China and the U.S.
19-kilometre bridge over Kerch Strait has been repeated target for Ukraine
Videos and images posted on X by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and verified by Reuters showed the bridge's main road arch had crumbled into the sea, leaving a yawning gap.
"Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges," Zelenskyy said. "We are ... reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began."
The 19-kilometre bridge is a flagship project inaugurated by Putin in 2018 and a symbol of Russia's attachment to the peninsula it captured and annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

The timing was awkward for the Kremlin leader ahead of his meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday with U.S. President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping, where the three are expected to discuss the Ukraine war among other topics.
Zelenskyy said the strike followed an unprecedented operation that methodically destroyed Russian air defences, radar systems and electronic warfare capabilities.
Sergei Aksyonov, Crimea's Russian-installed governor, said two people were killed and road traffic had been suspended. Rail traffic partially resumed after a pause.
Kremlin says Russia will rebuild bridge
Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a repair plan would be prepared, making the bridge "even better than before."
But Russian military bloggers said repairs would be exceptionally challenging given Ukraine's capacity for further attacks.
Finnish military analyst Emil Kastehelmi posted on X: "The road bridge won’t be repaired during this war ... Ukraine has achieved a victory with both concrete and symbolic implications."

The bridge over the Kerch Strait was once a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine, but the military now relies more heavily on a land corridor running through parts of eastern and southern Ukraine that Russia has captured since launching a full-scale war with its neighbour in 2022.
Ukraine strikes critical bridge in Russian-occupied Crimea

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin said a government commission had met to decide on steps to assess damage, launch repairs and discuss the logistics of delivering cargo to Crimea via alternative routes.
The bridge spans a channel used by commercial vessels entering and leaving the Sea of Azov, making it an important part of the region's grain export network.

While Black Sea grain shipments have largely stalled amid escalating drone attacks, export infrastructure has suffered limited damage, meaning trade could resume quickly if security conditions improve.

items: Russia says Ukrainian aerial attack involved more than 1,300 drones
Satellite limitations imposed by Musk's SpaceX pose danger for Ukraine, Zelenskyy says

blocks.text: Andrey Sizov, of consultancy Sovecon, said the bridge's collapse could "substantially delay any eventual resumption of shipping from the Sea of Azov" because debris would have to be cleared from the channel.

Ukraine has attacked the bridge several times during the war. A truck bomb in October 2022 killed four people and limited the bridge's capacity for several months. In July 2023, a section of road bridge was destroyed and a couple crossing by car were killed.
Largest Ukrainian drone attack

The overnight attack was part of what Russian state media called Ukraine's biggest drone attack yet. Russia said it shot down 1,441 drones over 22 regions, surpassing the previous record of 1,336 set on Monday.

Air defences repelled a major drone attack on the industrial cities of Ufa and Salavat in Russia's Bashkortostan region, home to several oil refineries, state media reported, citing local officials. Ukraine said it had hit a refinery and petrochemical complex in Salavat.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that around 800 Ukrainian drones had flown towards the surrounding Moscow region, 321 of which had been brought down en route.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on screen, addresses a meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group at NATO headquarters in Brussels on Tuesday. (Virginia Mayo/The Associated Press)

The scale and frequency of Ukrainian drone attacks have increased as Russia has intensified its own drone and missile campaign in a grinding war of attrition, with both sides targeting energy infrastructure and other strategic assets.
Attacks have continued despite U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week, the first in nine months, and separate meetings between U.S. envoys and Putin and Zelenskyy.

Kyiv and Moscow agreed on a major exchange of prisoners during last week's talks but there was no significant breakthrough on broader issues, including territory. Russia holds about a fifth of Ukrainian land but the front line has remained largely static for months.
Kyiv's bridges struck
In Kyiv, Reuters witnesses reported a series of loud explosions in the capital overnight.

Vitali Klitschko, Kyiv's mayor, said Russia struck the city's North and South bridges, an assertion later confirmed by Moscow, and partially damaged the metro system. The attacks caused some power and water outages and prompted transport restrictions, he said.
Overnight Russian strikes on energy infrastructure left consumers without power in eight Ukrainian regions, Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said.
Russia said its forces had struck transport, military and energy facilities in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk, along with port infrastructure and a cargo ship.
Reuters could not immediately independently confirm the reports. Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.

articles.title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
articles.summary: Moscow has targeted bridges in Kyiv, while Ukraine severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.
articles.byline: Sarah Rainsford, Mariana Matveichuk, Marianne Baisnee

blocks.text: The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.
Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.
Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.
At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.

The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.
Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.
Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.
Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.
"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.
But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.
"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."
From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.

A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.
Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.

The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.
On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.
"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."
That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.

Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.
Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.
To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.
But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.

The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.
"What else could I do?" she shrugged.
"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

articles.title: Costa Rican journalist shot dead in first such killing in 25 years
articles.summary:
Camilo Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence

The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against…

blocks.text: The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.

The first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years, ​Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long ⁠being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.
Rodriguez, 51, was attacked at about 3.20pm local ⁠time amid heavy traffic on a main highway on the outskirts of the capital ​San Jose, the Red Cross ‌reported.
President Laura Fernandez condemned ‌the attack in a video message.

“I am filled with indignation and outrage over ‌the cowardly murder of communicator Camilo Rodriguez. Regardless of the content of his communications, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression,” Fernandez said.

Attorney general Carlo Diaz told local news outlet Extra Noticias that investigators found multiple bullet impacts and a crime scene resembling a contract ‌killing, likely linked to the allegations Rodriguez had published. He gave no further evidence and did not name suspects.
“We know he ​was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking,” Diaz said, adding that Rodriguez had previously reported threats but had declined protection.
“Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a ⁠signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society.“
Diaz pledged efforts to ​hold those responsible ​for the murder accountable.

The last such ​attack on a media worker happened in July 2001 when radio ​producer Parmenio ‌Medina was gunned ​down on a ​Santo Domingo highway, in roughly the same area as Rodriguez’s attack took place.
Costa Rica’s homicide rate doubled between 2013 and 2023 and has only eased slightly since then.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia: Rights groups raise alarm over rising number of executions
articles.summary: Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving…

image.caption: Amid the ongoing conflict with Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen, Saudi Arabia cracks down on dissentImage: Vadim Nefedov/YAY Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.

The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.

In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.

"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.

According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM, the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.

blocks.caption: Saudi police forces reacted to peaceful protests by opening fire at the demonstrators in Quatif in 2011Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Is the Iran war affecting Saudi domestic repression?

Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.

"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Lea Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.
This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.

blocks.caption: Major sports events in Saudi Arabia are either postponed or canceled due to the ongoing attacks from Yemen's Houthis and Iran Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia's repression against the Shia minority

Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST, echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.

Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.

However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.

"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.
What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack?
DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

articles.title: Stolen 120-year-old church bell found discarded in rural Manitoba ditch
articles.summary: A heavy church bell stolen from the top of a belfry in rural Manitoba has been found abandoned in a ditch.

image.caption: RCMP Const. Merry Ploeg stands with the recovered church bell in the back of a police pickup truck on Tuesday. (Karen Pauls/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A heavy church bell stolen from the top of a belfry in rural Manitoba has been found abandoned in a ditch.
'Now we can kind of shift our focus over to figuring out who took it and how': RCMP
RCMP recovered it around 5:30 a.m. Tuesday near the small community of Malonton after receiving a tip from a passerby.
It was dumped about 10 kilometres southwest of the Sacred Heart of Jesus Ukrainian Catholic Church, which is 80 kilometres north of Winnipeg near Fraserwood.
It was stolen from the church during the week leading up to Nov. 14, when the theft was discovered, police said.
"That was a really unique piece of history, and we're just really relieved that it's been recovered and it's in good condition. It appears to be mostly undamaged," said RCMP Const. Merry Ploeg.
"Now we can kind of shift our focus over to figuring out who took it and how they took it. Even just recovering it took a few people, so it's quite a heavy piece of history."
Damage can be seen at the top of the wooden belfry. (Tyler Searle/CBC)

The bell, estimated to weigh about 135 kilograms (300 pounds), was somehow removed from a 1½-storey belfry that stands at the back of the Sacred Heart of Jesus churchyard in Manitoba's Interlake region.
Some boards were broken and removed from the top of the belfry, but how it was lowered is a mystery.
"That one … I haven't quite figured it out," said Ploeg.
There’s nothing on the ground to indicate where it might have landed if it was pushed out, and there are no tracks from any vehicles.

"I went over there and I was going over it pretty thoroughly just because, personally, I'd like to see if there's any cigarette butts left behind or anything that we could use as evidence. And I really wasn't finding anything," Ploeg said.
The bell from the Sacred Heart of Jesus Church is estimated to weigh more than 130 kilograms. Manitoba RCMP are still trying to figure out who took it and how. (Submitted by RCMP)
It was spotted in a ditch along Road 12 East by someone heading out to their hunting spot, she said.
Ploeg and the church parishioners were worried the ornate brass bell, which dates back to 1906, had been stolen to be sold to a scrapyard or melted down.
All the media attention the theft garnered likely scared the thieves off, said Ploeg, who believes they left it in a place where it could be found "so that they could get the heat off of them."

"Typically when we recover stolen property it'll be quite well hidden in the bushes or on properties, like rural areas, where people will stash them and wait until they can either use them or dispose of them another way or sell them or whatever," she said.

"The way that the bell was abandoned just in the ditch on the side of the road in plain view makes me feel very much that it was, like, purposeful. It wasn't stashed. It was left there to be found because now it's a hot item and it's all over the news."
The original church was built in Fraserwood in 1906. The current building was erected in 1942, two years after the original one was destroyed by a fire. (Tyler Searle/CBC)
The Interlake has large swaths of bushland and uninhabited areas where the thieves could have hidden the bell, Ploeg said.
"Even if you had a drone, what are the odds of you spotting it? It's the exact same colour as the grass [right now in fall]," she said.

items: 120-year-old church bell weighing 300 pounds stolen from belfry in rural Manitoba

blocks.text: The bell is now with the RCMP's forensics unit, which will be looking for fingerprints or other evidence that can be gathered from it.
Ploeg has spoken with representatives of the church to let them know it's been found.
The church isn't ready to take it back, anyway, because they need to do some repairs to the top of the belfry, where some of the wood was damaged during the theft, she said.
"So we'll give them some time to kind of figure that out and we'll make a plan of how it's going to be returned."
Gimli RCMP ask anyone with information about the theft or who may have seen anything suspicious in the area to contact the detachment at 204-642-5106.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.

articles.title: Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington
articles.summary: Tehran rejects any suggestion it was plotting a so-called dirty bomb attack on the US capital as "baseless".

blocks.text: President Donald Trump has said the US is taking "very seriously" the potential for any Iranian plot to attack Washington DC, after he was asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.

In the Philippines, where he attended the Asean Summit, Trump nodded when asked by a journalist about the report that Tehran was planning to detonate a so-called dirty bomb in the US capital and said: "We're looking into it."
CNN cited unnamed US intelligence officials suggesting Iran could target senior figures in Trump's administration with such an attack.
Iran called the claim "baseless." Concerns about dirty bombs grew after the 9/11 attacks in 2001, although no such attack has ever occurred.
Such a device would contain radioactive material - such as uranium - which would be scattered through the air when its conventional explosive detonated.
The BBC has not independently verified CNN's reporting.
During his comments to reporters in Manila, Trump was asked whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent.
"I hope it's not," he said, "but we take it very seriously because they [the Iranians] happen to be crazy."

In a statement before Trump's comments, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis wrote: "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei rebutted the CNN article and other US reports.
He posted on X: "Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations."
Mick Mulroy, a former CIA paramilitary officer and deputy assistant defence secretary, told the BBC: "A dirty bomb is not difficult to make or deploy."
"Although it is not a weapon of mass destruction, it can be a weapon of mass disruption," he added.

Imran Bayoumi, a geostrategy expert with the Atlantic Council in Washington DC and former policy adviser to the defence department, said that it remains "unclear how serious" would be the threat of a supposed Iranian dirty bomb.
"But Iran has planned and threatened to attack the US in the past," he said. "It is also unclear why this report is becoming public now."
It comes as intelligence officials and members of the Trump administration seek congressional renewal of a key national security law.
Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), which allows the US to ​spy on foreign nationals, expires next March.

articles.title: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play
articles.summary: Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump

blocks.text: Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long range drones.

The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

The collapse of a span of the roadway and the loss of its supporting arch above appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon,” says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe.

The 19km (12 mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula.

The Russian leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time.

That was four years before Putin’s full scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming.
Russia was able to bomb anywhere in Ukraine in 2022, while Kyiv was denied long range western missiles, particularly those powerful enough to strike such a politically sensitive and strategic target.

Instead, Ukraine tried to blow the bridge up with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone attack a year later. Neither did much long term damage. It was only as Ukraine’s own long range drones and cruise missiles came to fruition near the beginning of 2026 that a knockout strike became possible.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that the culminating attacks on the bridge, the end of two days of strikes, involved Ukrainian made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones plus Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus, the only foreign arms company confirmed as involved.

It was, the Ukrainian president said, the “seventh stage” in an operation “carried out over several weeks”. Radars, jamming equipment and air defence systems were progressively neutralised, opening up corridors of attack.

Meanwhile, Russia had already started what is becoming a battle of the bridges. Moscow attacked Kyiv’s busy Northern and Southern bridges in early October, part of its scaled up campaign against the capital and the country’s other large cities.

Russia is struggling to make progress on the frontline, and a record 50,000 troops were killed or seriously wounded in October, according to the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte. Its efforts are focused on knocking out Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water supplies, though attacking bridges show its target list is expanding in grim desperation.

Yet the Kremlin has chosen this expansion at a time when Ukraine can strike back. The pro-war Russian military blogger Military Informant notes that Ukraine has a “parity in firepower”, having downed the Kerch road bridge in two days of air raids. “It cannot be ruled out that the railway section will be destroyed next,” the blogger adds.

If anything, further attacks on the bridge are almost certain both to prevent its repair and to make resupplying Crimea more difficult. Cutting the bridge entirely, rail and road, would leave Moscow with only the R-280 land highway from Rostov to Crimea, already the subject of months of Ukrainian drone attacks.

Hodges has long argued that Crimea could be a defining theatre of the war, because “of what Crimea represents to Putin”. Ukraine should try to make “Russian occupation untenable” by destroying the bridge and asserting fire control over the R-280, he adds.

A supply squeeze, however, is a slow process, though its political benefits may be felt more quickly. Bringing down the road bridge “further kills the narrative that Russian victory is inevitable or that Crimea is theirs”, Hodges says, although Trump may not bring up the episode in his meeting with Putin and Xi on Thursday.

The danger is that both sides, in their desperation to end a deadlocked war, will escalate further. However, cut out of the talks in Shenzen, Zelenskyy had little choice but to remind Trump as well as Putin that Ukraine still has cards to play.

Emily Ferris, a Russia expert with the Rusi thinktank, says that Ukraine’s military-industrial complex was ready for some months, meaning the timing of the attack on the Kerch bridge can be interpreted only as political.
“They were keeping it for a rainy day, and that day has come,” she said.

articles.title: US and Mexico lose measles-free status
articles.summary: The United States lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization has said. Bolivia and Mexico have also lost their measles elimination status.

image.caption: Measles, a highly contagious virus, has spread in the US largely among the unvaccinated at the highest rate in more than 30 yearsImage: Sean Rayford/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The ​United States is experiencing its highest number ​of cases in more than three decades. Some 7,700 people in the country have been infected and 13 have died since 2025.

As ​of November 12, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have confirmed 5,412 measles cases and 6 deaths. US states have reported a total of 10 deaths from the highly contagious virus, this year.
Thanks to a series of functioning vaccines, measles had been virtually eradicated throughout most of the developed world for decades.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would return as Nvidia boss if asked by the board
articles.summary: Huang says he has had an "outpouring" of calls from investors and others calling for him to return.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang has said he would be "honored" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia, in his first public comments since his shock resignation after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.

In a statement shared with the BBC by a personal representative, Huang said: "I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely."
But he said he had had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia.
The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday.
The likelihood of Huang returning to the company is unclear, at best.
As the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board was not looking to bring him back into the company.
The board is actively investigating his conduct, which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive.
Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead.

articles.title: Krampus stirs up controversy in Ontario town after being banned from Santa Claus parade
articles.summary: Krampus, a European Christmas folk creature, has been banned from Strathory, Ont.,'s Santa Claus parade despite winning second place in the event's costume contest last year. Organizers say there…

image.caption: Krampus is the centre of controversy in Strathroy, Ont., after a local tattoo and piercing shop was told it wasn’t allowed to show off the European Christmas character at the town’s upcoming Santa Claus parade. (Submitted by Tanya Griffin)

blocks.text: London

Krampus, a European Christmas folk creature, has been banned from Strathory, Ont.,'s Santa Claus parade despite winning second place in the event's costume contest last year. Organizers say there were complaints that the figure wasn't "family friendly."
A tattoo shop in Strathroy, Ont., was told Krampus isn't allowed at parade
Although he has a long, white beard and is dressed in a red velvet suit, his pointy horns and gaping snarl indicate that he certainly is not Santa Claus.

Krampus, a terrifying counterpart to Saint Nicholas, is the centre of controversy in Strathroy, Ont., after the half-goat, half-demon European Christmas character was banned from the town’s upcoming Santa Claus parade.

“Everyone had spent so much time on their costumes and they were really excited. Even the children were pumped to be a part of this float,” said Tanya Griffin, the owner of Coven House, a Strathroy tattoo and piercing shop that entered Krampus in the parade.
“He was a celebrity. Everyone was cheering for Krampus,” she said of last year's float, which rode in last year's parade, where Krampus won second place in the a costume contest.
The shop was told last week that Krampus wasn’t allowed back at the parade, which is happening on Saturday, Griffin said.

Tanya Griffin is the owner of Coven House, a tattoo and piercing shop in Strathroy, Ont. An individual dressed as Krampus rode in Coven House’s Santa Claus parade float in 2025 and won second place in the parade’s costume contest. (Jessica Singer/CBC)
The decision was made by the Strathroy Lions Club, which runs the annual parade, after the group received complaints that Krampus wasn’t family-friendly, Griffin said.
CBC News has reached out to the local Lions Club but did not receive a response before publishing.
Krampus is ‘demonic,’ church says
Krampus is a Christmas monster with roots in European folklore whose job is to reprimand children who have misbehaved, said Griffin.
“He’s basically the guy that takes care of the naughty list,” she said.
Krampus appears in popular parades and Christmas events in Germany and other nearby European countries. A Lions Club chapter in Austria also hosts a Krampus event.

Although Krampus is often depicted as an evil or menacing demon in books and movies, Griffin said her intention was never to scare children. She said she wanted to educate the community about European Christmas traditions and folklore.
Krampus in Strathroy's 2025 Santa Claus parade. The character rode in Coven House’s float and won second place in the parade’s costume contest. (Submitted by Tanya Griffin)
Children were going to dress up as woodland creatures and march alongside Krampus as part of Coven House’s float this year, handing out candy canes and temporary tattoos to spectators, said Griffin.
“I think the most shocking part about all of this is the inclusivity and the discrimination part of it,” said Griffin.
“I feel like the Santa Claus parade should be about everything and everyone, and you shouldn’t be able to let one denomination, or one group, or one Krampus, out of it.”

items: Krampus, the European Christmas monster, is having a moment

blocks.text: CBC News obtained a letter written last year by the Calvary Church, a local Pentecostal church in Strathroy. Griffin said the letter was sent to the local Lions Club and delivered to her staff after last year’s parade.
In the letter, which is dated Dec. 10, 2025, the church writes that it was disappointed after satanic and demonic influences were promoted during the parade.
“Allowing the inclusion of satanic influences into what should have been a Christ-centred, Santa Claus Parade has caused a great displeasure,” the letter reads.
“To make matters worse, the parade judges awarded the float second place for costume and music, adding further insult as a result.”
The church was unable to provide an interview to CBC News, but said suggested Googling Krampus to "read the article of what he stands for...This will clarify our stand in the matter."
Brad Morrison is a minister at the Strathroy United Church. He said religion shouldn’t dictate what can be displayed at local parades. (Jessica Singer/CBC)

Brad Morrison, a minister at the Strathroy United Church, said religion shouldn’t dictate what can be displayed at local parades. He said he dropped by the tattoo parlour after hearing Krampus wasn’t allowed in the parade to offer his support.
“There are other groups in town that are rather vulnerable, and if they’re targeted next, where does it stop?” said Morrison.
“I know that religion can be toxic. I know that people can use their religion as an excuse to exclude others. And part of my job is to stand against that.”
It’s important for communities to receive education about how different cultures choose to celebrate Christmas, Morrison said.
“Change in a small town is slow, but time’s on our side,” he said. “We have a whole year of conversations about what are the values around cross-cultural understanding.”
The Santa Claus parade passes by Coven House on Frank Street, and on Saturday, Krampus will be standing outside her tattoo shop for spectators to see, Griffin said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jessica Singer is a CBC News journalist in London, Ont. She has also worked for the corporation from Toronto and St. John’s, N.L. Singer reported on the rise of far-right politics in eastern Germany as the 2026 recipient of the Gordon Sinclair Roving Reporter bursary. She was also named a 2025 FASPE fellow and a 2021 Joan Donaldson CBC News Scholar. You can reach her at jessica.singer@cbc.ca

articles.title: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers
articles.summary: States have reported over 5,400 cases and 10 measles-related deaths for the first time since the early 1990s.

blocks.text: After 26 years, the US has lost its status of having eliminated the highly contagious measles virus, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.
States have reported 10 measles-related deaths this year, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.

Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence of measles in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".
"These figures are a serious warning for our region," Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday.
He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.

Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said on Tuesday that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.
The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.
Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".
The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) did not respond to a request for comment from the BBC.

The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.
The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.

The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.

But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.

The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.
The country has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, the most it has recorded in a year since 1991.
An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.

US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.

Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.
Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.
The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.
Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.

President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine.
Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates.
"It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."
The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

articles.title: Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
articles.summary: The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

image.caption: Meeting of the North Atlantic Council at NATO headquartersImage: Stoyan Nenov/REUTERS

blocks.text: During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.
What does Russia mean by 1997?

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.
According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.
What would be the consequences of a NATO withdrawal?

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

blocks.caption: For more than 20 years, NATO allies have provided air policing over the Baltic statesImage: Arnaud Dumontier/MAXPPP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.
Why isn't the mutual-defense clause enough?

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

blocks.caption: Signing of the treaty establishing NATO in Washington on April 4, 1949Image: epa/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who decides which alliances a country can join?

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.
Was there a promise not to expand NATO eastward?

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

blocks.caption: In 2022, the last Russia Council meeting was held at NATO's headquarters in BrusselsImage: Olivier Hoslet/AFP

blocks.text: Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.
Why is the demand back on the table?

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: ‘We will have been spared a lot’: Kessler twins explained assisted dying decision in final letter
articles.summary:
Pop-singing sisters, who died together aged 89 last year, described declining health and expressed gratitude assisted dying was an option

Alice and Ellen Kessler, the identical pop-singing…

blocks.text: Alice and Ellen Kessler, the identical pop-singing twins who chose to jointly end their lives through assisted dying last year, said they had “reached rock bottom” due to health problems and had been relieved to be able to die together.
The sisters, who became huge television stars in the 1960s and 70s, especially in Italy and the US, said a catalogue of health conditions had left them with no desire to carry on living.

blocks.caption: Alice and Ellen Kessler in Erik the Conqueror in 1961. Photograph: Everett/Shutterstock

blocks.text: In a letter released by a friend, the 89-year-olds wrote: “Dear friends, we’re sorry that we’ve chosen to go this way, but due to our medical conditions we had no quality of life any more. Apart from our heart problems, we no longer have our senses of taste and smell. On top of that Ellen has suffered a brain stem stroke, and as a result we’ve reached rock bottom.”

blocks.caption: The twins performing in Paris. They became international stars through their singing and dancing, particularly on TV in Italy and the US. Photograph: Loomis Dean/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Because they had “entered the world together”, they wished “to depart it together the same way”, they added, concluding: “Don’t be sad; we’re happy that assisted dying exists, because certainly as a result we will have been spared a lot.”
They signed off: “Wishing you all the very best. We’ll see you on Cloud 9.”

The sisters died on 18 November last year , assisted by a doctor and a lawyer, in the villa they shared in the Grünwald district of Munich in Germany, which was divided into two mirrored halves, one for each. They had planned the process together, working with an assisted dying organisation, but had kept this from their friends.

The letters were posted into the letter boxes of people close to them on the evening before their deaths, with a handwritten instruction on the envelope: “Don’t open until 18 November.” Inside each envelope they had placed the gift of a piece of their jewellery.

Bibi Johns, a 97-year-old actor and the singers’ closest friend, the three having met on the set of the 1959 film La Paloma, said she heard of their deaths on the radio before she had had the chance to open the letter from them. “It was a shock,” she told the newspaper Bild. “Alice and Ellen were like sisters to me. For me it feels as if they have merely gone on a long journey. I’m still waiting for them to call me up.”
They bequeathed to her a gold pendant depicting the heads of two signs of the zodiac, a gift in 1968 from the French singer Marcel Amont to his then-partner Alice.

blocks.caption: An early publicity photograph. The sisters were inseparable and made a pact neither would marry. Photograph: ullstein bild Dtl./ullstein bild/Getty Images

blocks.text: The year before their deaths, in an interview with Italy’s Corriere della Sera, the sisters said their wish was “to leave together, on the same day … The idea that one of the two will go first is very difficult to bear.” In their lifetimes they had also made a pact that neither would marry.
