blocks.text: Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:
November 17, 2026
Rwanda migrant deportation hub scheme condemned by rights groups
A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.
The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.
The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."
Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.
"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.
"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."
In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.
"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.
"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.
Criticism from within the coalition

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).
"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.
"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.
"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."
Rwanda deportation hub planned for 2027
The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.
According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.
Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

articles.title: Tarriela rebuts Chinese scholar's claim that Ayungin Shoal is Chinese territory
articles.summary: Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela on Tuesday rejected a Chinese scholar's claim that Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal is Chinese territory, stressing that the disputed…

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 5:53pm

Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson Rear Admiral Jay Tristan Tarriela on Tuesday rejected a Chinese scholar's claim that Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal is Chinese territory, stressing that the disputed feature lies within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

Tarriela made the remarks after Dr. Zheng Zhihua of Shanghai Jiao Tong University argued that China was justified in using water cannons against Philippine vessels in the South China Sea, claiming that Beijing was merely defending its territory.

The exchange took place during a discussion on whether the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in the South China Sea should be legally binding.

Zheng said a COC would be ineffective without a fundamental consensus among China and ASEAN member states. He cited what he described as a key disagreement, claiming that the Philippines had been occupying Second Thomas Shoal, which he called Chinese territory, for 27 years.
He also defended China's use of water cannons against Philippine fishing and coast guard vessels operating within the Philippines' EEZ.
"China only uses water cannons as a big power. I think if other countries occupy your land territory, you only use water canals to defend your territory integrity," Zheng said.
Tarriela disputed the professor's assertion.
"I would just like to correct you in saying that China does not have any territorial jurisdiction whatsoever in Second Thomas Shoal," he said.

"The last time I checked, Second Thomas Shoal only has a distance of 125 nautical miles from the Philippines. And it is our exclusive economic zone, not China's," Tarriela added, citing the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which provides for an EEZ extending up to 200 nautical miles from a country's baselines.
Zheng countered by saying: "No country occupied Second Thomas Shoal as easy like Philippines did."
Indonesian scholar Dr. Dewi Fortuna Anwar, meanwhile, said ASEAN should intervene to help defuse tensions in the South China Sea.
Anwar said China should reach out to ASEAN member states rather than assert its power, warning that displays of might would not resolve territorial disputes.
"To jeopardize the goodwills of ASEAN countries over these issues in the South China Sea, I think is, you know, you are shooting your foot," she said.

In July 2016, an arbitral tribunal under the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines in its case against China, rejecting Beijing's expansive claims over much of the South China Sea based on its nine-dash line.
The tribunal also ruled that areas of the Spratly Islands, including Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Reed Bank, are within the Philippines' EEZ and continental shelf.

It further found that China had unlawfully prevented Filipino fishermen from accessing Scarborough Shoal, also known as Panatag Shoal, which it recognized as a traditional fishing ground for both Filipino and Chinese fishermen.
The ruling stemmed from an arbitration case initiated by the Philippines in 2013. China refused to participate in the proceedings and has rejected the ruling.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Trump arrives in Manila for state visit, ASEAN-US Special Summit
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump will also meet with fellow Quad leaders in Manila where protests against Pax Silica and the US war on Iran await him

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – US President Donald Trump arrived in Manila late Tuesday afternoon, November 17, for a state visit and to participate in the ASEAN-US Special Summit and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) leaders’ summit on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit.

Trump arrived in Manila amid protests from groups opposed to his policies, especially the US war on Iran and his administration’s vaunted Pax Silica initiative. Hundreds had been arrested in relation to the protests that began on November 15, the opening of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.

Before Trump’s late afternoon arrival on Tuesday, ASEAN leaders held meetings with Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, Chinese Premier Li Qiang, and Indian President Narendra Modi, ahead of the annual East Asia Summit.
Trump skipped the East Asia Summit but will join a US-ASEAN Special Summit as well as the Quad leaders’ summit, both scheduled after the conclusion of the ASEAN Summit.

The meeting of the Quad — the US, Japan, Australia, and India — will be Trump’s first and takes place two years after the last gathering of the group, which his predecessor Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.

It comes just ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping who previously objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing. Quad members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.

On Wednesday, November 18, Trump will have bilateral meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Malacañang, to be followed by a state luncheon in his honor before he departs for the APEC Summit in Shenzen.

Trump’s Asia trip, which also includes a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts in Shenzen, comes after his Republican Party’s defeat in midterm elections and spy allegations that could complicate a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China. – With reports from Reuters/Rappler.com

articles.title: House leader confident Congress will pass 2027 budget on time, avert reenactment
articles.summary: A leader of the House of Representatives expressed confidence that the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 would be approved on time, ruling out the possibility of a reenacted budget.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 5:30pm
A leader of the House of Representatives expressed confidence that the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 would be approved on time, ruling out the possibility of a reenacted budget.
The House of Representatives approved the proposed 2027 national budget on third and final reading in October. The measure is now undergoing review in the Senate.

"That's the worst thing that can happen, reenactment. I believe we are on the right track in terms of pacing," House Committee on Appropriations vice chairperson Zia Alonto Adiong said in an online interview on Tuesday.
"The Senate is multitasking, doing the impeachment and the budget at the same time. There's nothing to worry about the budget being reenacted because they have set their timeline," he added.
Once the Senate approves its version of the budget, the differences between the House and Senate versions will be reconciled by the bicameral conference committee.
Congress is scheduled to go on Christmas recess on December 19, 2026, with sessions set to resume on January 17, 2027.

Adiong said any possible delay in the budget's approval would likely last only a few days, adding that lawmakers could adjust the session schedule to accommodate the ratification of the bicameral conference committee report.
"The most that we can actually expect as to the possible delay is only a few days. At puwede naman din po magkaroon ng adjustment doon sa session days para po sa ratification ng bicam," he said.
Meanwhile, Adiong said the House is working on establishing a transparency website that would allow the public to monitor government project funding and implementation.
The proposed platform was earlier announced by House Speaker Faustino Dy III.
"Ongoing po yung pagpu-put up nitong website na ito for each, for the succeeding years to come," Alonto Adiong said.

He added that the public would be able to access information on projects during the budget season, including their identification in each congressional district and their subsequent implementation. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Indian woman gang-raped while pregnant in 2002 'heartbroken' after two perpetrators bailed
articles.summary: Bilkis Bano has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" at the top court order and vowed to fight back.

blocks.text: The article has details that some readers may find disturbing

A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.
Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.
The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.
All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.

In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.
The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".
On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".

"She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."
Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".
The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.
Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.
When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child.
They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she'd told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.

items: How a Gujarat riot victim stood up to her rapists
India Supreme Court cancels release of 2002 riots rapists
India PM Modi's government okayed rapists' release

blocks.text: Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.
Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.
Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.

Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.
In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief".
"I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said.

"For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."
Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives".

"I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.
In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

House Impeachment Trial spokesperson Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong on Tuesday called on the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte to report to the authorities the alleged threat received by one of her former household staff.

Adiong said this after Duterte's spokesperson, Atty. Paolo Panelo, said the vice president received a message yesterday from the staff member, asking for help and rescue. The whereabouts of the former household staff member is unknown.

articles.title: Fear, outrage grow as Quebec moves to ban religious symbols for elementary students
articles.summary: Quebec parents of young children who wear religious symbols are worried about the new PQ government’s proposal to ban elementary school students from wearing such symbols at school. Experts say there…

image.caption: Mehwaish Raja's 11-year-old daughter started wearing a hijab to elementary school this fall. Raja says she doesn't think the government should decide what her daughter wears to school. (Steve Rukavina, CBC News)

blocks.text: Mehwaish Raja’s 11-year-old daughter surprised her during a conversation this past summer on the way to day camp.
“She shared with me during the car ride: ‘Mama, I will wear my hijab at the end of the summer,’” Raja said.
Up until that point, her daughter only wore the hijab for special occasions, and Raja had never insisted she wear it regularly.
“I just said, ‘OK.’ And by the end of the summer, it actually happened,” Raja said.
Her daughter now wears the hijab every day in her Grade 5 class in a public school in Montreal’s West Island.
Now, the new Parti Québécois government is proposing a law that would make that practice illegal as part of a series of measures announced on the campaign trail to strengthen secularism.

items: Groups decry Quebec's proposed ban on school kids wearing religious symbols

blocks.text: Raja is struggling to understand why.
“Honestly, I'm out of words. I'm out of words when I hear things like this,” she said.
She doesn’t think the government should be able to decide what her daughter wears to school.
“When we step out of our house, we leave as who we are. What part of us do we leave at home?” she said.
Parents, experts raise concerns over Quebec’s proposed ban on school kids wearing religious symbols
Religious symbols gradually squeezed out of schools

The previous CAQ government already introduced several laws restricting religious symbols in schools, preventing at first teachers, and then all school staff – even parent volunteers – from wearing them.

Generally, religious symbols bans in Quebec have targeted employees of the state considered to be in positions of authority, but the CAQ opened the door to targeting students by introducing a ban on full face coverings at school.
Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is opening that door wider, proposing a blanket ban preventing elementary school students from wearing "conspicuous" religious symbols while at school.

“Separating children through what they wear and through religious beliefs at such a young age is not helping cohesion and integration,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in September when announcing the measure, without providing any specific examples.
“We think it's a good policy in terms of letting children just be children, with no connection whatsoever to what their parents believe about religion,” he'd said.

When proposing the religious ban for elementary schools during the election campaign, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said the symbols 'interfere with cohesion and integration.' (Ivanoh Demers/CBC/Radio-Canada)
Winning a minority government in the general election did not soften the PQ's resolve, with new Education Minister Joël Arseneau saying the measure was a "non-negotiable."
"It’s on this basis that we were elected, and it’s on this basis that we’re working,” Arseneau told reporters at the National Assembly in late October.
Mother says proposed law based on misconceptions
Asma Qureshi says the PQ's proposal comes from a place of ignorance.

Qureshi, who lives on Montreal’s South Shore, has four children. Her oldest daughter, now in high school, started wearing a hijab to school when she was in Grade 4. Her youngest daughter, currently in kindergarten, wore one to school a couple of times this year just to try it.
Qureshi – who wears a hijab herself – says in both cases, she didn’t ask or order her daughters to wear one.
"I told myself that I would never impose it on my kids," she said.
"There’s this narrative that goes around – and it's been there since I was a young kid – that children and women are being forced to wear the scarf."

items: Quebec’s secularism laws upended their lives. They fear what comes next could be worse

blocks.text: Qureshi thinks that misconception is what’s feeding the gradual tightening of restrictions on wearing religious symbols in Quebec, particularly in schools.
She says she hasn’t yet discussed the proposed ban with her daughters.
“How do you tell a child it’s against the law for you to wear something that your mother wears?” she said.
Raja says her daughter's decision to start wearing the hijab regularly this fall convinced her to do the same. (CBC News)
For Raja, who up until now had been reluctant to wear a hijab in Quebec for fear of standing out, says her daughter's decision to wear one at school this fall convinced her to do the same.
“I'm really proud of her because at 11 years old, she decided to wear it, whereas I’m 40 and I hadn't been able to,” she said.
“My daughter truly inspired me."
Ban would cause harm, experts say
Experts in secularism and child development told CBC there is no justification for banning students from wearing religious symbols — and that the measure would be harmful.

Thomas Dee, an economist at Stanford University who specializes in how education policy affects student outcomes, disagreed with the notion of asking children to leave their parents' religious baggage behind.
“Parents are children's first and most impactful teachers, and to sideline their guidance and insights just seems misguided to me and disrespectful,” he said.
Dee testified as an expert witness in the court challenge to Bill 21, Quebec’s first secularism law.

Thomas Dee, an economics professor at Stanford University who studies the effects of education policy on student outcomes, says a policy that marginalizes parents' values in school is misguided and disrespectful. (CBC News)
Sivane Hirsch, a professor in the faculty of education at Université Laval who specializes in cultural and religious diversity in schools, believes the ban is a horrible idea.
“We don’t want children to feel they’re being taught in school against their parents, against their family,” Hirsch said.
Dee said such a conflict would also hurt students’ performance.
“Anything that makes students feel less welcome or less at ease will imply they're not able to bring their full attention and motivation to the realization of their academic potential,” Dee said.

items: Gatineau mom told she can't wear hijab at after-school event: parent committee

blocks.text: Zeinab Diab, a religious studies researcher at Université de Montréal and author of Au nom de la laïcité, a book about Islamophobia in Quebec, said a secularism law that targets young children is inhumane.
“They are dehumanizing them and limiting their access to school. What kind of society allows that?” she said.
Author and religious studies researcher Zeinab Diab says targeting children for a religious symbols ban is inhumane. (CBC News)
Dee said the presence of religious symbols in the classroom could actually help.
“If you engage with people across difference, you no longer use simple rules of thumb to judge them, but rather you judge them as people,” he said.
Qureshi said that was her daughter’s experience.
She said no other students made negative comments or gave her daughter a hard time when she started wearing the hijab.
“It was just like she was any other regular person,” she said. “That's the beautiful thing – when people can recognize you for who you are rather than what you wear."
PQ needs support of at least 1 other party
In order to adopt the ban, the PQ will need support from at least one other party in the National Assembly.
Charles Milliard, leader of the Quebec Liberals and the Official Opposition, said last week his party wouldn’t support the measure.
“We're talking about children. I'm not going to do politics on the backs of children,” Milliard said.
Québec Solidaire also doesn’t support the measure.
That leaves the Conservative Party of Quebec.
On Monday, leader Éric Duhaime said his party generally supports secularism, but wanted to see more details before deciding whether to support the proposed law.
"I mean, what are we going to do with those kids if they don't respect the rules?" Duhaime told reporters.
"That's the kind of thing that I want to know before we move forward."
Education Minister Joël Arseneau says he's negotiating with other parties about the idea of banning religious symbols for elementary school students, and that their positions may evolve. (CBC News)
Last week, Arseneau said he was in negotiations with other parties about the bill, and that their positions may evolve. He declined CBC’s request for an interview.
The Canadian Civil Liberties Association issued a statement Tuesday calling on all members of the National Assembly to oppose the idea regardless of of their political affiliation.

"Children’s access to education should never be conditional on whether the government approves of their religious identity or expression," Harini Sivalingam, director of equality for the CCLA, said in the statement.
"Schools should be places where children learn, develop their identities and build relationships with others from different backgrounds," Sivalingam said.
"You cannot promote inclusion by excluding children,” she said.
Raja says if the ban does become law, her daughter would likely leave her current school.
“If the public system is really asking us not to practise certain values that we strongly believe in, I would choose another way of educating my children,” she said.
For her that would likely be private school, but she said some other parents might choose homeschooling.
Diab said not all families have either the money or the time for those options.
“Maybe they’re going to adapt, but no one should be always in fight and survival mode,” she said.
“This is exhausting.”

articles.title: ASEAN leaders sign new power grid deal. What’s next for Philippines?
articles.summary: Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin says the ADB and World Bank have 'indicated their interest in financing' regional power grid connections, which could require hundreds of billions of dollars…

blocks.text: ASEAN. Energy ministers from different ASEAN member-states pose ahead of discussions on regional energy issues, on October 7, 2026.
ASEAN

Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin says the ADB and World Bank have 'indicated their interest in financing' regional power grid connections, which could require hundreds of billions of dollars in investment

items: All 11 ASEAN countries have signed an Enhanced Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on the ASEAN Power Grid, aiming for an interconnected electricity network to facilitate cross-border electricity trade.

The agreement focuses on infrastructure planning, policy development, and financing, with significant potential benefits for the Philippines, including improved electricity reliability and reduced reliance on fossil fuels.

Challenges include the need for substantial investments in infrastructure and the integration of power markets, with ASEAN targeting fully integrated operations by 2045, although no firm construction timetable has been established.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Southeast Asian nations have long dreamed of an interconnected electricity network. Now, they are one step closer after all 11 ASEAN countries completed the signing of a power grid agreement that could eventually allow them to buy and sell electricity across borders.
The Enhanced Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on the ASEAN Power Grid officially entered into force upon completion of its signing on Sunday, November 15, during the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila.

According to ASEAN, the agreement “covers cooperation on infrastructure planning, institutional arrangements, policy and regulatory development, and access to financing, including for overland transmission lines and subsea power cables.” (Watch ADB’s brief explainer video below:

The agreement builds on discussions during the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu last May, when leaders pushed for greater regional energy connectivity, particularly through submarine power cables connecting the region’s island economies. This continued during the ASEAN energy ministers’ meeting in Manila last October, when all member countries at the time reached a consensus on the agreement.
With all ASEAN countries now manifesting their support for an interconnected grid, the proposal now moves down to the more detailed technical, legal, and financial levels of discussion.

blocks.caption: Rappler Recap: Myanmar, South China Sea among issues as 49th ASEAN Summit opens

blocks.text: For the Philippines, the benefits could be significant. Connecting to neighboring countries could allow the country to import electricity when domestic supplies are tight. Beyond improving reliability, it could also help move the Philippines’ away from expensive and dirty fossil fuel generation. (READ: Solar for whom? What Philippines can learn from Pakistan’s rooftop boom)
But connecting the grids will be neither cheap nor easy.

The Philippines itself operates three major electricity grids, Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, which are now interconnected but still face transmission constraints. It was only in 2023 that the P52-billion Mindanao-Visayas Interconnection Project was energized, allowing electricity to flow between the two regions.

Even this year, the Visayas and Mindanao grids have repeatedly been placed under yellow and red alerts, with parts of the Visayas experiencing rotational power outages. These shortages were caused mainly by power plant outages, compounded by transmission constraints that capped the amount of electricity the Visayas could import from Luzon.
Connecting the Philippines to the rest of ASEAN would no doubt require another major investment in submarine cables, alongside improvements to domestic transmission infrastructure.

The costs could be substantial. According to the International Energy Agency, ASEAN would need around $27 billion in investment in cross-border power interconnections from 2025 to 2040, on top of more than $300 billion needed to expand and modernize domestic electricity grids. ASEAN’s own estimate is even higher, at $764 billion covering both power generation and transmission through 2045, assuming high adoption of renewable energy.

The regional bloc knows this well, which is why its enhanced MOU encourages pooling resources among governments, the private sector, and financial institutions to finance power grid projects. This is complemented by the ASEAN Power Grid Financing Initiative, which brings together ASEAN, the Asian Development Bank, and the World Bank to help prepare projects and mobilize funding.

Energy Undersecretary Felix William Fuentebella said that investors will view the signing of all ASEAN members in the enhanced MOU as a strong positive sign, which could unlock “big amounts of investments” and pave the way for more detailed feasibility studies on interconnections. Energy Secretary Garin also said that the ADB, World Bank, and other development-focused financial institutions have “indicated their interest in financing this” depending on the project proposal.

blocks.caption: ASEAN leaders sign new power grid deal. What’s next for Philippines?

blocks.text: Another major challenge could be power market integration, which ASEAN said would follow a “voluntary, stepwise approach” that takes into account policies, laws, and regulations of the participating countries.

“It will be by steps, voluntary – because we won’t be forcing any country that will not participate,” Garin told Rappler in a press conference on Tuesday, November 17. “But with the signature of everyone in the enhanced MOU, that’s a clear indication already of their participation.”
ASEAN is targeting fully integrated regional electricity grid operations by 2045, although individual connections could be developed earlier.

However, for now, no firm construction timetable has been set, with ASEAN acknowledging that “further development of technical, regulatory and commercial frameworks will be essential to translate this foundation into bankable investments.”

On November 15, the Philippines’ Department of Energy also separately signed a two-year research agreement with the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, which includes technical studies supporting the Philippines’ participation in the regional grid. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: 'Europe needs to wake up' to realise defence costs if Ukraine fails, Danish minister says
Danish defence minister Jeppe Bruus has warned that “Europe needs to wake up” as “the price, if Ukraine falls, will be lot higher than the amount we are now delivering for Ukraine.”

blocks.caption: Denmark's defence minister Jeppe Bruus Photograph: Ida Marie Odgaard/Reuters

blocks.text: “Ukraine has the most efficient and also modern army in all of Europe. We are gaining a lot of advantages [from] the cooperation with the Ukrainians,” he said.
But he added that “the cost of Ukraine losing will be a lot higher” than any current aid given to Kyiv.
Germany to contribute $300m for US air defence systems for Ukraine ahead of 'exceptionally difficult winter', Pistorius say

German defence minister Boris Pistorius has warned that Ukraine is facing “an exceptionally difficult winter” amid intensifying Russian attacks on critical infrastructure as he confirmed Germany will fund a new package of air defence systems for Kyiv.

blocks.caption: Germany's defence minister Boris Pistorius speaks with the media as he arrives for a meeting of EU defense ministers at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AP

blocks.text: “Ukraine is facing an exceptionally difficult winter as Russia is doing everything in its power - and will continue to do so – to destroy Ukraine’s water, electricity and energy infrastructure,” he said.
Pistorius said that Russia was “intensifying its aerial assaults because its if failing to make progress on the battlefields.”
“For us, as nations supporting Ukraine, this means one thing clearly: we must continue to provide effective and rapid support for Ukraine’s air defence,” he said.
Germany will contribute $300m for another round of defensive weapons purchases from the US, with Norway also expected to join.

“Supporting Ukraine is not an act of charity. It is about far more than solidarity or assisting a nation under attack; it is about the security of Europe – and, by extension, about stopping Putin and keeping him in check.”
During the Ukraine defence contact group, which Pistorius co-chairs, the EU ministers will be joined by the US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby.
“This is important, as we have several matters to discuss – for instance, the upcoming Force Posture Review, as well as cooperation on defence equipment and various other topics.”
Morning opening: Ukraine hits crucial bridge linking Russia and Crimea

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

blocks.caption: Gallen section of Kerch Bridge after it was hit by Ukrainian drones. Photograph: Ukrainska Pravda

blocks.text: Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.
But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

“We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders ‌for repair work. We are sorting out logistics issues with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.
The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine ​and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.
The overnight strike followed ‌an intensification of ​Russian attacks in the ​past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.
Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.
Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.
They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.
It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: PNP: No formal report yet on alleged threat reported by Sara Duterte's camp
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Tuesday it has not received any formal report regarding an alleged threat against a former household helper of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 4:32pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Tuesday it has not received any formal report regarding an alleged threat against a former household helper of Vice President Sara Duterte.

PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co was asked about the claims of Duterte's lawyer Paolo Panelo that the household staff asked the vice president for help as she was allegedly being held against her will and was being forced to sign a document.
"Have they reported it to us? To the Philippine National Police? As of this time, we have received no reports that they have reported it to us," Co said at a press briefing.
Co pointed out that the PNP could not initiate an investigation based solely on social media posts containing unverified allegations.
He encouraged the vice president or anyone with information about the alleged threat to report the matter directly to the PNP.

According to a Facebook post by Atty. Paolo Panelo, Duterte's spokesperson, the vice president received a message at 11:19 p.m. on Monday "from what appeared to be the account of a former household staff member" asking for help and rescue in Manila.

The sender claimed to be under the custody or control of certain individuals who allegedly threatened their life. The former staff member also said they were being forced to sign a document but refused to do so.
Panelo said the person's whereabouts remain unknown and their safety and well-being have yet to be verified.

Panelo expressed concern that the incident could be part of what he described as a campaign by the Marcos administration to allegedly harass and coerce individuals into becoming false witnesses against Duterte amid her impeachment trial.
For its part, Malacañang said authorities should investigate the matter to determine the truth behind the Duterte camp's claims.

Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro shrugged off Panelo's statement that the alleged incident may be part of the administration's supposed campaign against Marcos, saying the President was busy with the ongoing 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: China taps US AI models to train homegrown rivals as chip curbs bite
articles.summary: China's use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced chips to China, as its developers can build AI capabilities by drawing on those of their American…

blocks.text: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE. An AI sign is seen at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, China on July 6, 2023.
Aly Song/Reuters

China's use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced chips to China, as its developers can build AI capabilities by drawing on those of their American rivals

items: Chinese entities are increasingly using distillation techniques to leverage output from American AI models, aiming to enhance their domestic AI capabilities amid tightening US restrictions on chip access.

Research indicates this practice has moved from academic settings to mainstream industrial applications, with Chinese companies automating processes and training smaller models based on American outputs.

The growing use of distillation raises geopolitical tensions, as US officials express concerns over potential intellectual property theft and the effectiveness of US chip export controls, while Chinese developers seek clarity on the legality of their practices.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BEIJING, China – Chinese entities are adopting increasingly sophisticated ways to use output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals, documents show, as China aims to broaden its AI strategy and offset tightening US curbs on its access to chips.

A Reuters review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices and government documents reveals how the practice — known as distillation — has expanded beyond academic experiments into mainstream industrial use in China.

The records describe Chinese researchers using US models to produce answers to questions, build computer code, and find solutions to difficult problems, with Chinese companies then developing software to automate the process and specialist workers preparing material for training smaller domestic models.
The documents also show that Beijing is encouraging distillation to make AI cheaper and easier to deploy across China’s powerful manufacturing sector.

Distillation is not illegal and is prevalent in other parts of the world. While the process cannot reproduce a leading model’s full capabilities or eliminate the need for advanced computing power, it can help developers preserve selected skills in smaller systems that cost less to operate, potentially reducing their reliance on American technology.

China’s broadening use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced chips to China, as its developers can build AI capabilities by drawing on those of their American rivals. Washington said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to such chips from companies like Nvidia.

Distillation is also a source of friction between the world’s two biggest economies ahead of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are expected to meet.
US authorities publicly accused Chinese companies in September of aggressive, targeted distillation of American AI models on an industrial scale.

And at meetings in Chengdu in July, US Commerce Department officials raised concerns with Chinese regulators about developers collecting output from leading American AI models, warning that some activities could amount to intellectual-property theft, three people familiar with the discussions said.

Chinese officials defended distillation as a standard AI-development technique and said they were open to acting where the conduct constituted IP theft, but made no concrete commitments, according to a US official familiar with the previously unreported exchange.
The US Commerce Department and China’s Cyberspace Administration did not respond to requests for comment.
Distillation involves a powerful ‘teacher’ model generating answers or demonstrating how to complete tasks, which developers use to train a smaller ‘student’ system.

For Chinese developers facing constraints on computing power, the attraction is in making one expensive query do repeated work, according to a former Alibaba Group engineer who spoke on condition of anonymity. An American model can generate the answer to a difficult question once, allowing a Chinese team to retain useful examples and train a local system around them.

In a November 2024 paper, Shanghai Jiao Tong University researchers described selecting about 5,000 answers from OpenAI’s o1 model, translating them using GPT-4o mini and assembling 10,750 bilingual training examples to further train Alibaba’s Qwen2.5-72B model.
The researchers also cautioned that excessive reliance on distillation could stifle original innovation, leaving developers dependent on breakthroughs made by more advanced model providers.
The project illustrated how American model output can become reusable data, allowing developers to improve domestic systems without repeatedly consulting the original provider.

Alibaba researchers described a more systematic approach in an April 2025 paper, using OpenAI’s GPT-4 and GPT-4o to generate training material in languages other than Chinese, then refining and scoring responses before training smaller Qwen models.

In a February 2026 paper, researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Chinese food-delivery company Meituan described using GPT-4o to generate plans for coordinating AI agents working together on programming problems, helping train a smaller model to organise such tasks.
Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Alibaba and Meituan did not respond to requests for comment.

Among leading American AI companies, OpenAI’s terms restrict using its output to develop competing models, subject to exceptions, while Anthropic similarly restricts training competing systems without permission.

A US official familiar with the July Chengdu regulatory discussions said Washington believes industrial-scale distillation is the main reason Chinese AI models have narrowed the gap with their American rivals.
Two people familiar with Chinese developers’ operations disputed that assessment, saying distillation was only one factor alongside advances in engineering, algorithms, data and model design.
Chinese government documents do not instruct companies to distil American models but encourage distillation as part of Beijing’s push to spread AI across the world’s second-largest economy.

A national AI+Manufacturing policy package published by eight Chinese government agencies in January includes guidance supporting model training, fine-tuning and distillation for industrial applications. Shanghai and Shenzhen have also encouraged techniques to reduce computing requirements.
The policies reflect Beijing’s ambition to deploy smaller, cheaper AI systems across industries.

Concerned by distillation’s growing geopolitical sensitivities, Chinese AI developers have in recent months asked Beijing’s industry regulator for guidance on the boundaries between ordinary use of foreign models and organised collection of output for training, according to one person familiar with the discussions.
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to a request for comment. – Rappler.com

articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes
articles.summary:
As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here

The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to…

blocks.text: The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.

India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.

So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.

My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.

Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’

blocks.caption: Memorable … the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh. Photograph: Sumit Kumar/Getty Images

blocks.text: One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.

Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.

The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.

The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.

For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.

The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’

blocks.caption: Overtourism is a real risk in places like Goa. Photograph: Pavel Laputskov/Getty Images/iStockphoto

blocks.text: The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.

But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.

Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.

Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.

Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.

Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
after newsletter promotion
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: The Congress party, led Rahul Gandhi, says one-third of delegates at its summit in Hyderabad at the weekend were denied entry to India. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.

Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.

Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: A screenshot from I Am 20, an inventive documentary short film from 1967. Photograph: YouTube

blocks.text: Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Post-Diwali pollution near President’s House in New Delhi. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: In We Were Here, humans are trying to take AIs’ jobs. Photograph: Sunshine Motion Pictures

blocks.text: AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.

articles.title: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact
articles.summary: Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join the next round of demonstrations ahead of the US president’s arrival in Manila for the Asean summit

blocks.text: Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests ahead of the US president’s arrival in the city for a leaders’ summit.

Organisers claim as many as 10,000 people will join protests against Trump in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, when he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds are expected to try to walk to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.

Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “number one terrorist” in protests held on Monday.

Demonstrators angry at the cost-of-living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.

Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon, and public holidays instituted for the Asean summit.

Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The backlash against Trump follows the ouster of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump’s delegation was expected to include businessman Elon Musk.

Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said.
“Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”

blocks.caption: Indigenous communities and other groups protest in Manila on Monday.  Photograph: Nathaniel Soriano/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 120km from Manila.

Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 25 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty Philippines said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” director Ritz Lee Santos III said.
“Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

articles.title: European-made pesticides named in 1,605 poisoning reports in Brazil last year
articles.summary:
About a third of cases involved chemicals banned for use on EU farms, according to investigation by Unearthed and Public Eye

Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in…

blocks.text: Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found.

About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.

Analysis of Brazilian health ministry data by Unearthed and Public Eye in a report published on Tuesday found that of 2,857 poisoning reports that named an identifiable agricultural product, 1,605 named brands sold by European pesticide companies.

Farm workers in Brazil have described their flesh rotting, skin burning, difficulty breathing and vomiting after using the chemicals at work, according to the report. A small number have died accidentally or killed themselves by drinking the pesticides.

Under Brazilian law, reports must be submitted by healthcare professionals to Brazil’s national disease notification system in all suspected pesticide poisoning cases. These reports can be marked “confirmed” poisoning or “exposure” only by the doctor or nurse who saw the patient.

blocks.caption: A worker in protective gear rinses gloves under water near a pesticide warning sign in Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Clinicians sometimes record cases as exposure when they lack the training or support to confirm a diagnosis, but are presented with a patient who says they have been exposed to pesticides or present symptoms of pesticide poisoning. Laboratory confirmation is rare, so recording a diagnosis of “confirmed” poisoning usually depends on clinical judgment.
Experts say clinicians can be reluctant to confirm cases because of a lack of training or support. A brand being named in a poisoning report is not proof that it caused poisoning or death.

“The insufficient training of healthcare professionals to recognise and manage these cases is a major limiting factor,” said Vanda Garibotti, a public health biologist at the State Centre for Health Surveillance in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil.
High staff turnover and a lack of institutional support meant poisoning cases were rarely confirmed through laboratory tests and often relied on clinical judgment, Garibotti added.

In more than 6,700 medical reports involving agricultural pesticides last year, 2,857 named an identifiable product. Of those, 1,420 were classified as confirmed poisonings. A further 1,108 were classified as exposures; for the remainder the classification was unknown or other diagnoses.

Some of the products are made in Britain. Reglone is the most frequently cited UK-made weedkiller. It contains diquat, a chemical that was banned in the UK in 2020 after experts concluded it posed a high risk to people living near fields where it was sprayed. Diquat is also found in other pesticides.

Despite the usage ban, Reglone is still manufactured by the Swiss-headquartered pesticides company Syngenta at its factory in Huddersfield for export to countries with more permissive regulations, including Brazil.

blocks.caption: A mass is held in honour of Nelson Castoldi in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Nelson Castoldi died last year after accidentally ingesting Reglone on his family farm in Rio Grande do Sul. To save money, his family had bought the weedkiller in bulk, decanting a single litre into an empty cola bottle to avoid hauling a heavy 20-litre canister into the fields.

Working under the scorching sun, Castoldi mistook the black chemical for a soft drink and took a sip. Though he spat it out immediately, the chemical caused his kidneys to fail before attacking his lungs. He died two days later.

“We fell apart,” Ivan Castoldi said of his father’s death. “Four months after our father passed away, our mother also passed away. She cried day and night. She became depressive and had a stroke. She was left alone.
“That poison, Reglone, should be banned in Brazil,” he added. “Not because of what happened to us, but because of its toxicity.”
The Brazilian health ministry recorded 75 cases involving diquat last year, compared with 36 over the five years from 2018 to 2022.

The investigation found Reglone was specifically named in 44 reports, including four deaths. Of those cases, 26 were classified as confirmed poisonings and the rest were classified as exposure, unknown, or adverse reaction.
Dormex, a pesticide manufactured in Germany by Alzchem and distributed in Brazil by the German chemical company BASF, is another product workers said injured them or made them ill.

blocks.caption: Sidnei Souza de Oliveira, 49, suffered a severe injury after a jug of Dormex spilled on his leg while he was filling a sprayer. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Sidnei Souza de Oliveira, 49, suffered a severe injury after a jug of Dormex spilled on his leg while he was filling a sprayer. The handle broke as he was transferring the chemical into the tank. At first, his leg turned red, and he continued spraying.

He carried on working for four days before going to hospital. “After 15 days, my leg was black. Chunks of flesh were falling off,” Oliveira said. A doctor said the injury was serious and had to remove dead tissue to stop it spreading towards the bone.

Oliveira said the protective trousers supplied by his employer were thin and allowed the chemical to seep through. He said he had been afraid of losing his job if he stayed away from work for too long.

Dormex contains cyanamide, which was banned from use in the EU in 2008 because of concerns about its effects on human health, particularly among farm workers spraying the chemical. Analysis shows the Brazilian health ministry database recorded 17 confirmed poisonings involving Dormex last year.

Finale, a BASF product identified in the investigation, contains glufosinate, which was banned in the EU in 2018. Roundup – a glyphosate-based weedkiller manufactured by the German chemical company Bayer – was frequently cited in Brazilian poisoning reports, including 12 deaths.

Across all the poisoning reports identified by the investigation as involving products sold by European companies, there were 32 reported deaths. Of these cases, 31 were classified as confirmed poisonings, and 26 were recorded as suicides.

Syngenta products were cited 425 times in the poisoning reports, and BASF 179 times. The company figures are not mutually exclusive: some poisoning reports named products sold by more than one manufacturer.
Nina Schrank, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace UK, said the findings were a “deadly double standard”.

“If a pesticide is too dangerous to use in Britain, it should be too dangerous to export. Ministers must stop allowing Britain to be part of a production line for toxic chemicals that are putting lives at risk overseas.”

blocks.caption: Empty pesticide containers in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: The EU’s pesticide approval system requires chemicals to meet strict standards for human and animal health and the environment. Diquat has been banned on EU and UK farms since 2019 and 2020 respectively, after experts concluded it posed a high risk to workers, people living nearby and birds. Cyanamide was withdrawn after an assessment found exposure among agricultural operators could exceed safe levels. Glufosinate, meanwhile, is classified in the EU as toxic to reproduction, meaning it can harm fertility or the development of unborn children.

Suicide prevention is also a factor. A 2020 study found national bans on highly hazardous pesticides could be a cost-effective intervention for reducing the number of people who kill themselves in countries with a high burden of suicides attributable to pesticides.

A Syngenta spokesperson said almost half the Brazilian cases attributed to the company were not classified as confirmed poisonings, adding: “Public Eye and Unearthed are aware of this but have explicitly chosen to disregard the dataset’s final classification.” The company accused the investigation of disregarding the dataset’s final classifications and identified “numerous other inconsistencies” that it said raised “serious concerns” that the evidence was “being selectively interpreted to support a predetermined conclusion”.
“There are real people behind these statistics. Every genuine case of poisoning matters, and every family affected deserves our concern,” the spokesperson added.

Syngenta said Brazil had its own “robust regulatory system” and that products banned in Europe could still be independently assessed and legally registered in the country, citing differences in crops, growing conditions and pest pressures. It said it trained 95,000 people in Brazil in the safe use of its products in 2025, including through free online courses.

blocks.caption: Pesticide are sprayed in an apple orchard in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Bayer said its products were safe when used according to label instructions, citing what it described as rigorous testing and assessments by global health authorities. The company said it took pesticide poisoning seriously but questioned the reliability of the data, arguing that products and circumstances of exposure had not been independently verified, some chemicals may have been incorrectly identified and symptoms such as headaches and skin irritation could have other causes.
It said “Roundup” was “widely used as a generic term” that could refer to weedkillers made by other manufacturers or counterfeit products.

The company said it provided training on the safe handling and use of pesticides, including protective equipment, and that its programmes reached more than 4 million people globally in 2025. It also argued that a pesticide being banned in the EU did not necessarily mean it was unsafe, saying other countries had robust regulatory systems that took account of local agricultural conditions.

It added: “While the data presented helps to provide information on broad trends of exposure, the data has limitations and warrants caution when drawing conclusions, particularly when looking at individual cases.”
BASF said it was deeply concerned by reports of poisoning that might be linked to its products, adding that it took all such incidents seriously.

A spokesperson said publicly available information suggested some incidents might have involved the intentional ingestion of crop protection products, describing such acts as “deliberate misuse” of products intended exclusively for agricultural use.

BASF said it had global and local procedures to assess and investigate incidents potentially involving its products, and worked with authorities and experts where appropriate to understand cases and identify ways to prevent similar incidents. It said it invested in education and training to promote the safe handling and use of its products, with initiatives in Brazil reaching more than 14,475 participants in 2025.
The company said it was confident in the safety of its products when used in accordance with label instructions and applicable regulatory standards.

It added that Brazilian law required crop protection products to be handled and applied only by authorised and properly trained individuals, and said it took its responsibility for ensuring their safe use seriously.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
articles.summary: Efforts to recover bodies after a “double-tap” attack in southern Ukraine are being hampered by continuing Russian strikes, officials say.

blocks.text: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images
ByMerlyn Thomas BBC Verify correspondent and Paul BrownBBC Verify
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there have been multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged.
"Due to the threat of repeated shelling, emergency workers are constantly forced to periodically suspend work and retreat to a safe place," it added.
The DSNS said the death toll had risen to at least 72 people making it one of the deadliest single incidents since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted

blocks.text: Image source, DSNS
Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

blocks.caption: Emergency services workers leave a rubble filled area in Ukraine

blocks.text: Bodies are still to be recovered from the rubble, Oleksiy said. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead."
BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.

blocks.caption: Map of southern and eastern Ukraine showing areas under Russian military control and the location of Komyshuvakha, a village on the southern front line in Zaporizhzhia region. Russian-controlled territory is shaded pink, with limited Russian control shown by red hatching and claimed Russian contr…

blocks.text: A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.
Fears of second strike heard on police radios

Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.
Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in Ukraine
Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.
Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.

blocks.caption: Satellite image showing the site of the Komyshuvakha attack in Ukraine. White annotations highlight a large rectangular compound and surrounding buildings. A white dot marks the reported impact point inside the compound, while brackets indicate access points on the western side of the site. Two n…

blocks.text: The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.
Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.

Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.

blocks.caption: The crater was identified by experts as consistent with a 3,000kg bomb
